questions.q: What best describes machine learning (ML)?
options: A subset of AI where systems learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions
A field where computers follow explicitly hand-coded rules for every decision
A statistical technique that only works on numerical spreadsheet data
A hardware architecture designed specifically for faster computation
questions.explanation: Machine learning is a branch of AI in which algorithms learn patterns from data rather than being explicitly programmed with rules.

questions.q: How does artificial intelligence (AI) relate to machine learning?
options: AI is a narrower subfield contained entirely within ML
ML is a subset of the broader field of AI
AI and ML are two completely unrelated fields
AI only refers to robots with physical bodies
questions.explanation: Machine learning is one approach within the broader field of artificial intelligence, which also includes rule-based systems and other techniques.

questions.q: In supervised learning, what does the training data contain?
options: Only input features with no known outcomes
Rewards and penalties from an environment
Input features paired with known correct labels or outcomes
Randomly generated synthetic values only
questions.explanation: Supervised learning trains on labeled examples where each input is paired with its known correct output.

questions.q: Which scenario is a classic example of unsupervised learning?
options: Predicting a household's income from survey answers using labeled data
Training an agent to maximize rewards through trial and error
Forecasting rainfall from historical labeled weather records
Grouping villages into segments based on similarities without predefined labels
questions.explanation: Unsupervised learning finds structure such as clusters in unlabeled data without predefined output labels.

questions.q: Reinforcement learning is best characterized by which mechanism?
options: Learning by trial and error through rewards and penalties from an environment
Learning from a fixed dataset of labeled examples
Grouping unlabeled data into clusters
Reducing the number of features in a dataset
questions.explanation: Reinforcement learning trains an agent to take actions that maximize cumulative reward through feedback from its environment.

questions.q: An M&E team wants to predict whether a beneficiary will drop out of a program (yes/no). This is an example of which task?
options: Regression
Classification
Clustering
Dimensionality reduction
questions.explanation: Predicting a discrete category such as yes/no dropout is a classification task.

questions.q: Predicting the number of years of schooling a child will complete (a continuous number) is an example of which task?
options: Classification
Clustering
Regression
Reinforcement learning
questions.explanation: Predicting a continuous numeric value is a regression task.

questions.q: In machine learning terminology, what is a 'feature'?
options: The correct answer the model is trying to predict
The overall accuracy of the model
The algorithm used to train the model
An individual measurable input variable used to make predictions
questions.explanation: A feature is an input variable (such as age or income) used by the model to make predictions.

questions.q: In supervised learning, what is a 'label'?
options: The known correct output or target value for a training example
An input variable fed into the model
The name given to the dataset file
A tuning parameter of the algorithm
questions.explanation: A label is the known correct output (target) associated with each training example in supervised learning.

questions.q: Why is a dataset typically split into training, validation, and test sets?
options: To make the dataset smaller and faster to load
To train, tune, and then honestly evaluate the model on data it has not seen
Because algorithms can only read data in three parts
To duplicate the data three times for backup
questions.explanation: Splitting lets you train the model, tune it on validation data, and get an unbiased performance estimate on unseen test data.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of the test set?
options: To adjust the model's parameters during training
To select which features to include
To provide an unbiased estimate of performance on unseen data
To increase the size of the training data
questions.explanation: The test set is held out and used only once to estimate how the model performs on new, unseen data.

questions.q: What does overfitting mean?
options: The model performs poorly on both training and test data
The model has too few parameters to capture the pattern
The model was trained on too much data
The model learns the training data too well, including noise, and fails to generalize
questions.explanation: Overfitting occurs when a model memorizes noise in the training data and performs poorly on new data.

questions.q: What does underfitting mean?
options: The model is too simple to capture the underlying pattern in the data
The model memorizes the training data perfectly
The model performs perfectly on test data but not training data
The model has too many features
questions.explanation: Underfitting happens when a model is too simple to capture the true relationship, performing poorly even on training data.

questions.q: A model shows very high accuracy on training data but much lower accuracy on test data. This most likely indicates:
options: Underfitting
Overfitting
A perfectly generalized model
That the test set is too large
questions.explanation: A large gap between high training accuracy and low test accuracy is the classic signature of overfitting.

questions.q: In a classification context, what does accuracy measure?
options: The proportion of predicted positives that are truly positive
The proportion of actual positives correctly identified
The proportion of all predictions that are correct
The average error in continuous predictions
questions.explanation: Accuracy is the fraction of all predictions (both positive and negative) that the model got right.

questions.q: What does precision measure in a classification model?
options: Of all actual positive cases, how many were predicted positive
The total fraction of correct predictions
The difference between predicted and actual values
Of all cases predicted positive, how many are actually positive
questions.explanation: Precision is the proportion of positive predictions that are actually correct (true positives / predicted positives).

questions.q: What does recall (sensitivity) measure?
options: Of all actual positive cases, how many the model correctly identified
Of all cases predicted positive, how many are truly positive
The overall accuracy across all classes
How fast the model makes predictions
questions.explanation: Recall is the proportion of actual positive cases that the model correctly identifies (true positives / actual positives).

questions.q: The F1 score is best described as:
options: The simple average of accuracy and recall
The harmonic mean of precision and recall
The total number of correct predictions
The square root of the accuracy
questions.explanation: The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing the two into a single metric.

questions.q: Why can accuracy be misleading when detecting a rare outcome (e.g., 2% of beneficiaries defaulting)?
options: Accuracy cannot be calculated for rare events
Accuracy only works for regression tasks
A model predicting 'no default' for everyone would still score 98% accuracy while missing all defaults
Rare events make accuracy impossible to interpret
questions.explanation: With imbalanced classes, a naive model can achieve high accuracy while failing to detect the rare class of interest.

questions.q: When is machine learning generally NOT the appropriate tool?
options: When patterns are complex and buried in large amounts of data
When predictions must be made on new incoming data
When there is abundant labeled historical data
When the problem can be solved reliably with a few simple, known rules
questions.explanation: If a problem is solvable with simple deterministic rules, ML adds unnecessary complexity and is not the right tool.

questions.q: Which of the following is a clustering task?
options: Segmenting survey respondents into natural groups without predefined categories
Predicting whether a loan will be repaid
Estimating a household's monthly expenditure
Ranking students by predicted exam score
questions.explanation: Clustering groups data points into natural segments based on similarity, without using predefined labels.

questions.q: In the context of ML, what is a 'model'?
options: The raw dataset used for training
A learned mathematical representation that maps inputs to outputs
A physical server running the computation
The person who labels the data
questions.explanation: A model is the learned function or representation that maps input features to predicted outputs.

questions.q: What is the role of the validation set?
options: To provide the final unbiased performance estimate
To serve as additional training examples only
To tune hyperparameters and make model selection decisions during development
To store the labels separately
questions.explanation: The validation set is used during development to tune hyperparameters and compare models without touching the test set.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches learning type to data requirement?
options: Supervised learning requires unlabeled data
Unsupervised learning requires labeled data
Reinforcement learning requires a fully labeled dataset
Supervised learning requires labeled data
questions.explanation: Supervised learning requires labeled data, while unsupervised learning works on unlabeled data.

questions.q: A false negative in a program-dropout predictor means:
options: Someone who will actually drop out is predicted as not at risk
Someone who will not drop out is flagged as a dropout risk
The model correctly identifies a dropout
The model correctly identifies a non-dropout
questions.explanation: A false negative is when an actual positive case (a real dropout) is incorrectly predicted as negative (not at risk).

questions.q: A false positive in a fraud-detection model means:
options: A genuine fraud case is missed
A legitimate case is incorrectly flagged as fraud
A legitimate case is correctly cleared
A fraud case is correctly caught
questions.explanation: A false positive occurs when a negative (legitimate) case is incorrectly predicted as positive (fraud).

questions.q: In a health screening tool where missing a true case is dangerous, which metric should be prioritized?
options: Precision
Training speed
Recall
Number of features
questions.explanation: When missing true positives is costly (e.g., missed disease cases), recall (catching actual positives) should be prioritized.

questions.q: What is a confusion matrix?
options: A chart of the model's training loss over time
A list of all features ranked by importance
A matrix used only in unsupervised learning
A table showing counts of true/false positives and negatives for a classifier
questions.explanation: A confusion matrix tabulates true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives to summarize classifier performance.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best example of a good ML use case for an M&E team?
options: Predicting which schools are at highest risk of low attendance from many historical indicators
Adding two budget columns together in a spreadsheet
Counting how many surveys were submitted today
Converting currency using a fixed exchange rate
questions.explanation: ML excels at finding complex patterns across many variables, such as predicting risk from historical indicators, unlike simple arithmetic tasks.

questions.q: What does 'generalization' refer to in machine learning?
options: A model's ability to memorize the training set
A model's ability to perform well on new, unseen data
The process of collecting more data
The speed at which a model trains
questions.explanation: Generalization is a model's ability to perform accurately on data it has not seen during training.

questions.q: Which technique helps reduce overfitting?
options: Adding more noise to the training labels
Removing the test set entirely
Using regularization or gathering more diverse training data
Increasing model complexity without limit
questions.explanation: Regularization and more diverse training data constrain the model and improve generalization, reducing overfitting.

questions.q: In predicting a continuous outcome, which is a common evaluation metric?
options: Precision
Recall
F1 score
Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
questions.explanation: Regression models are evaluated with error metrics like Mean Absolute Error, whereas precision/recall/F1 are for classification.

questions.q: What is a 'target variable' in supervised learning?
options: The variable the model is trained to predict
Any input feature in the dataset
The learning rate of the algorithm
The size of the training set
questions.explanation: The target variable (also called the label or dependent variable) is what the supervised model is trained to predict.

questions.q: Semi-supervised learning is best described as:
options: Learning using only fully labeled data
Learning using a small amount of labeled data combined with a large amount of unlabeled data
Learning purely from environmental rewards
Learning without any data at all
questions.explanation: Semi-supervised learning combines a small labeled dataset with a larger pool of unlabeled data to improve learning.

questions.q: Data leakage in ML refers to:
options: Losing data files due to storage failure
Sharing datasets with unauthorized users
Information from outside the training data (or the target) improperly influencing the model
Compressing data too aggressively
questions.explanation: Data leakage occurs when information not legitimately available at prediction time leaks into training, giving overly optimistic results.

questions.q: Why is class imbalance a concern in classification?
options: It makes the dataset impossible to split
It always causes underfitting
It prevents features from being used
The model may ignore the minority class while still scoring high accuracy
questions.explanation: With imbalanced classes, a model can achieve high accuracy by favoring the majority class while failing on the minority class.

questions.q: A 'hyperparameter' is:
options: A configuration setting chosen before training that controls the learning process
A value learned automatically from the data during training
The final prediction output
A synonym for a feature
questions.explanation: Hyperparameters (like learning rate or tree depth) are set before training and govern how the model learns, unlike parameters learned from data.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a regression problem in M&E?
options: Classifying households as poor or non-poor
Predicting a district's exact vaccination coverage percentage
Grouping communities into unlabeled clusters
Deciding whether a grievance is resolved or not
questions.explanation: Predicting a continuous percentage value is a regression problem, while the others involve categories or clusters.

questions.q: Cross-validation is used primarily to:
options: Permanently increase the dataset size
Replace the need for any test set forever
Obtain a more reliable performance estimate by rotating training and validation splits
Label unlabeled data automatically
questions.explanation: Cross-validation rotates which subsets serve as training and validation, giving a more robust estimate of model performance.

questions.q: When precision and recall trade off against each other, F1 is useful because it:
options: Always equals the higher of the two
Ignores recall entirely
Only reflects accuracy
Combines both into a single balanced measure
questions.explanation: F1 balances precision and recall into one number, useful when you must weigh both types of errors.

questions.q: Which statement about labeled data in development contexts is accurate?
options: Obtaining high-quality labels can be costly and time-consuming, limiting supervised learning
Labeled data is always freely available for any outcome
Labels are never needed for supervised learning
Labels only matter for unsupervised learning
questions.explanation: Acquiring reliable labels (e.g., verified poverty status) is often expensive and slow, which constrains supervised ML in the field.

questions.q: What is 'feature engineering'?
options: Deleting the target variable from the dataset
Creating or transforming input variables to improve model performance
Choosing the number of test samples
Deploying the model to production
questions.explanation: Feature engineering is the process of creating, selecting, or transforming input variables to help the model learn better.

questions.q: If a model performs poorly on both training and test data, the most likely diagnosis is:
options: Overfitting
Perfect generalization
Underfitting
Data leakage
questions.explanation: Poor performance on both training and test data indicates the model is too simple to capture the pattern, i.e., underfitting.

questions.q: Which of the following best distinguishes classification from regression?
options: Classification predicts continuous numbers; regression predicts categories
Both always predict the same type of output
Classification requires no labels; regression requires labels
Classification predicts discrete categories; regression predicts continuous numbers
questions.explanation: Classification predicts discrete class labels while regression predicts continuous numeric values.

questions.q: An M&E officer wants to automatically group thousands of open-ended survey comments into themes without predefined categories. This is:
options: Unsupervised clustering
Supervised classification
Regression
Reinforcement learning
questions.explanation: Grouping data into emergent themes without predefined labels is unsupervised clustering.

questions.q: What does it mean that a model has 'bias' in the statistical ML sense (bias-variance)?
options: The model is unfair to certain groups only
The model makes systematic errors due to overly simplistic assumptions
The model memorizes noise in the data
The model has too many parameters
questions.explanation: In the bias-variance sense, high bias means the model's simplistic assumptions cause systematic errors (linked to underfitting).

questions.q: High variance in a model typically corresponds to:
options: Underfitting and overly simple assumptions
A model that ignores the training data
Overfitting and sensitivity to fluctuations in the training data
A perfectly calibrated model
questions.explanation: High variance means the model is overly sensitive to the training data's noise, which corresponds to overfitting.

questions.q: Before deploying an ML model for M&E decision-making, a key ethical consideration is:
options: Whether the model runs on the fastest hardware
Whether the code uses the newest programming language
Whether the model file is small enough to email
Whether the training data may embed bias that leads to unfair predictions for certain groups
questions.explanation: Biased or unrepresentative training data can produce unfair predictions, a critical ethical concern before deployment.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of a typical supervised ML workflow?
options: Collect and label data, split it, train on training set, tune on validation, evaluate on test
Evaluate, then collect data, then train
Train on the test set, then collect data
Deploy first, then gather features
questions.explanation: The standard workflow is to collect/label data, split it, train, tune on validation, and finally evaluate on the held-out test set.

questions.q: For a program targeting scarce resources where every flagged case is manually verified at high cost, which metric matters most to avoid wasted verification effort?
options: Recall
Precision
Training time
Number of clusters
questions.explanation: When each positive prediction triggers costly follow-up, high precision minimizes false positives and wasted effort.

questions.q: At the most basic level, what does a large language model (LLM) like the one powering a chatbot actually do when generating text?
options: It looks up pre-written answers stored in a database
It predicts the next token (piece of text) based on the preceding text
It searches the live internet for the best matching sentence
It runs a fixed decision tree of if-then rules
questions.explanation: LLMs generate text by repeatedly predicting the most likely next token given the preceding context, one token at a time.

questions.q: In the context of LLMs, what is a 'token'?
options: A security key needed to access the model
A unit of text such as a word or part of a word that the model processes
A payment credit charged per conversation
A hidden watermark added to generated text
questions.explanation: A token is a chunk of text (a word, sub-word, or character) that is the basic unit an LLM reads and generates.

questions.q: Roughly how many tokens does a typical English word correspond to in most modern LLMs?
options: About 0.75 tokens per word (words are often a bit less than one token)
Exactly 1 token per letter
About 10 tokens per word
Tokens have no relationship to words
questions.explanation: As a rough rule, one English word averages about 1.3 tokens, so a token is often slightly smaller than a word.

questions.q: What is the 'context window' of an LLM?
options: The physical screen area where the chat appears
The maximum amount of text (tokens) the model can consider at once
The time window during which the model is available
The number of users who can chat simultaneously
questions.explanation: The context window is the maximum number of tokens (input plus output) the model can take into account in a single interaction.

questions.q: An M&E officer pastes a very long evaluation report into a chatbot and the model seems to 'forget' the beginning. What is the most likely cause?
options: The report exceeded the model's context window
The model is broken and needs reinstalling
The internet connection dropped
The model only reads the last sentence by design
questions.explanation: When input exceeds the context window, earlier content is truncated or dropped, so the model appears to forget it.

questions.q: In LLM terminology, what is a 'hallucination'?
options: A visual image the model generates
When the model produces confident but false or fabricated information
A deliberate error message shown to users
A slowdown when the server is overloaded
questions.explanation: A hallucination is when an LLM generates plausible-sounding but factually incorrect or invented content.

questions.q: Which practice best reduces the risk of acting on a hallucinated fact when using an LLM for M&E work?
options: Always trust the most detailed answer
Verify specific facts, figures, and citations against original sources
Increase the temperature setting
Ask the same question in a louder tone
questions.explanation: Because LLMs can fabricate details, verifying key facts and citations against primary sources is essential.

questions.q: What does the 'temperature' setting control in an LLM's text generation?
options: The processing speed of the model
The randomness or creativity of the output
The physical temperature of the server hardware
The length of the response in words
questions.explanation: Temperature controls output randomness: lower values make responses more focused and deterministic, higher values more varied.

questions.q: For an M&E task that needs consistent, factual, reproducible outputs (like extracting indicators from reports), which temperature setting is generally most appropriate?
options: A high temperature to maximize creativity
A low temperature for more deterministic output
Temperature has no effect on factual tasks
The maximum possible temperature
questions.explanation: A low temperature yields more consistent and predictable outputs, which suits extraction and factual tasks.

questions.q: What is an 'embedding' in the context of LLMs and AI?
options: A numerical vector representation of text that captures meaning
An image embedded inside a document
A code snippet embedded in a webpage
A password protecting the model
questions.explanation: An embedding is a numeric vector that represents text so that semantically similar text has similar vectors.

questions.q: Why are embeddings useful for semantic search over a collection of M&E documents?
options: They compress files to save disk space
They let you find documents by meaning, not just exact keyword matches
They translate documents into other languages automatically
They encrypt the documents for security
questions.explanation: Embeddings enable semantic similarity search, retrieving conceptually related content even when exact words differ.

questions.q: What does RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) do?
options: It retrains the model on new data every night
It retrieves relevant documents and supplies them to the LLM to ground its answer
It randomly generates text without any input
It rates the quality of generated answers
questions.explanation: RAG fetches relevant source documents and feeds them into the model's context so answers are grounded in that material.

questions.q: A primary benefit of using RAG for an organization's M&E knowledge base is that it:
options: Eliminates the need for any human review
Grounds answers in your own documents, reducing hallucination and adding citations
Makes the model run without any internet
Permanently teaches the model your data through training
questions.explanation: RAG grounds responses in provided documents, which reduces hallucination and lets answers cite specific sources.

questions.q: In a RAG system, does answering a question with your documents change the underlying model's trained weights?
options: Yes, each query retrains the model
No, the documents are supplied at query time as context, not used to retrain
Yes, but only for embeddings
No, because RAG deletes the model after each use
questions.explanation: RAG injects retrieved text into the prompt context at query time; it does not alter the model's trained parameters.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a chatbot and an AI agent?
options: A chatbot uses text and an agent uses only voice
An agent can take actions and use tools to complete multi-step tasks, not just converse
A chatbot is always more accurate than an agent
There is no difference; the terms are identical
questions.explanation: An agent can plan, call tools, and take actions across steps to achieve a goal, whereas a chatbot mainly responds in conversation.

questions.q: Which of the following is the most accurate description of how LLMs are initially trained?
options: By memorizing a fixed list of question-answer pairs
By learning statistical patterns from very large amounts of text data
By copying answers directly from Wikipedia only
By being manually programmed with grammar rules
questions.explanation: LLMs are pretrained on massive text corpora, learning statistical patterns of language rather than memorized Q&A pairs.

questions.q: Why might an LLM be unaware of very recent events (for example, a policy change last week)?
options: It refuses to discuss politics
Its training data has a cutoff date, so it lacks knowledge past that point unless given new context
Recent events are too complex for any AI
It only knows information from its home country
questions.explanation: A base LLM's knowledge is frozen at its training cutoff; recent information must be supplied via context or tools.

questions.q: Which statement about LLMs and arithmetic is most accurate?
options: LLMs are perfectly reliable calculators
LLMs can make arithmetic mistakes because they predict text rather than truly computing
LLMs cannot handle numbers at all
LLMs always call a calculator internally
questions.explanation: Because LLMs generate text by prediction, they can produce arithmetic errors and are not guaranteed calculators.

questions.q: A common misconception is that an LLM 'understands' text the way a human does. A more accurate view is that it:
options: Consciously reasons about meaning like a person
Models statistical relationships in language to produce useful outputs
Retrieves the single true answer from a fact database
Feels emotions about the content
questions.explanation: LLMs model statistical patterns in language; they do not possess human-like conscious understanding or emotions.

questions.q: What is a 'prompt' in the context of using an LLM?
options: The input text or instruction you give the model
The waiting time before a response appears
An error warning displayed to the user
The model's internal training algorithm
questions.explanation: A prompt is the input text or instruction provided to the model to elicit a response.

questions.q: What does 'prompt engineering' refer to?
options: Building the physical servers that run models
Crafting and refining inputs to get better, more reliable outputs from an LLM
Writing the code of the model itself
Encrypting prompts for security
questions.explanation: Prompt engineering is the practice of designing effective inputs to guide the model toward useful, accurate outputs.

questions.q: Providing a few worked examples inside a prompt to guide the model's response is known as:
options: Zero-shot prompting
Few-shot prompting
Fine-tuning
Overfitting
questions.explanation: Few-shot prompting includes example input-output pairs in the prompt to steer the model's behavior.

questions.q: Asking an LLM to answer a task with no examples, relying only on instructions, is called:
options: Few-shot prompting
Zero-shot prompting
Retrieval-augmented generation
Batch processing
questions.explanation: Zero-shot prompting gives only an instruction without examples, relying on the model's pretrained abilities.

questions.q: What is 'fine-tuning' an LLM?
options: Adjusting the volume of the audio output
Further training a base model on additional specialized data to adapt its behavior
Writing a longer prompt
Restarting the model when it freezes
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning continues training a pretrained model on task- or domain-specific data to adapt its outputs.

questions.q: For an M&E team that just wants grounded answers from its own reports without heavy technical setup, which approach is usually simpler than fine-tuning?
options: Building a new model from scratch
Using RAG to supply relevant documents at query time
Manually memorizing all reports
Increasing the temperature to maximum
questions.explanation: RAG grounds answers in your documents without the cost and complexity of retraining or fine-tuning a model.

questions.q: Which of these is a genuine limitation of current LLMs that M&E practitioners should keep in mind?
options: They can guarantee 100% factual accuracy
They can produce confident-sounding but incorrect outputs
They never need any human oversight
They always cite their sources correctly
questions.explanation: LLMs can output confident but wrong information, so human oversight and verification remain necessary.

questions.q: Why should sensitive beneficiary data be handled carefully before pasting it into a public AI chatbot?
options: The text may be too long to process
The data could be transmitted to and potentially retained by a third party, raising privacy concerns
Chatbots cannot read personal names
It will slow down the response time
questions.explanation: Pasting sensitive personal data into a public tool can expose it to third parties, so data protection and consent matter.

questions.q: What does it mean that LLM outputs can be 'non-deterministic'?
options: The model never produces the same answer twice under any setting
The same prompt can yield different responses, especially at higher temperature
The model determines everything with certainty
Outputs are always identical regardless of settings
questions.explanation: LLM generation can vary between runs due to sampling randomness, especially at higher temperature settings.

questions.q: Which best describes 'multimodal' AI models?
options: Models that only work in multiple languages
Models that can process more than one type of input, such as text and images
Models running on multiple servers
Models with multiple pricing tiers
questions.explanation: Multimodal models handle multiple input/output types, for example combining text, images, or audio.

questions.q: An M&E officer wants an LLM to summarize 200 field interview transcripts consistently. Which factor most directly limits how much of each transcript the model can consider at once?
options: The temperature setting
The context window size
The number of distractor options
The embedding color
questions.explanation: The context window caps how much text the model can process in one pass, limiting how much of each transcript fits.

questions.q: Which statement about LLM 'confidence' is most accurate?
options: A fluent, assertive answer is proof it is correct
Fluency and confident tone do not guarantee factual accuracy
The model always warns you when it is wrong
Confidence scores are always shown to users
questions.explanation: LLMs can sound highly confident while being wrong; tone is not a reliable indicator of correctness.

questions.q: What is 'chain-of-thought' prompting?
options: Linking multiple chatbots together
Encouraging the model to work through reasoning steps before giving a final answer
A method for encrypting prompts
Chaining multiple users into one session
questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to reason step by step, which can improve performance on complex tasks.

questions.q: Why can two different LLMs give different answers to the same M&E question?
options: They were trained on different data and have different architectures and settings
One is always lying
The internet changes their answers
Only the newest model can ever be correct
questions.explanation: Different models differ in training data, size, architecture, and configuration, so their outputs can diverge.

questions.q: In RAG, what is typically stored in a 'vector database'?
options: The raw model weights
Embeddings of document chunks used to retrieve relevant text
User passwords
The chatbot's chat history only
questions.explanation: A vector database stores embeddings of document chunks so semantically similar chunks can be retrieved efficiently.

questions.q: What is 'chunking' in a RAG pipeline?
options: Deleting parts of documents at random
Splitting documents into smaller passages before embedding and retrieval
Compressing the model
Merging all documents into one file
questions.explanation: Chunking breaks documents into manageable passages so relevant pieces can be embedded and retrieved precisely.

questions.q: Which is a realistic and appropriate use of an LLM in M&E work?
options: Automatically approving budget disbursements with no review
Drafting a first version of an interview coding scheme for a human to refine
Serving as the sole source of official statistics
Replacing all field verification
questions.explanation: LLMs are well suited to drafting and assisting tasks that a human then reviews, not to making unreviewed final decisions.

questions.q: What does 'grounding' an LLM response mean?
options: Disconnecting the model from electricity
Basing the answer on provided, verifiable source material
Making the answer shorter
Translating the answer into a local language
questions.explanation: Grounding ties the model's answer to specific supplied sources, improving reliability and traceability.

questions.q: A colleague claims 'the AI searched the whole internet in real time to answer.' For a standard offline LLM without web tools, this is:
options: Correct, all LLMs browse live
Incorrect; a base LLM answers from patterns learned in training, not live browsing
Correct only on weekends
Incorrect because LLMs cannot read
questions.explanation: A base LLM responds from its trained parameters, not live web access, unless explicitly connected to search tools.

questions.q: What is a practical risk of relying on an LLM to cite academic references for an evaluation report?
options: It may invent plausible-looking but non-existent citations
It always formats citations perfectly
It cannot produce any citations
Citations slow down the model
questions.explanation: LLMs can fabricate realistic but fake citations, so references must be checked against real sources.

questions.q: Which setting or approach would you adjust to make an LLM's outputs MORE varied and exploratory for brainstorming survey questions?
options: Lower the temperature toward zero
Raise the temperature
Shrink the context window
Remove the prompt
questions.explanation: Higher temperature increases randomness and variety, which can help with brainstorming and idea generation.

questions.q: What does 'token limit' most directly affect in a practical sense?
options: The color scheme of the interface
How much text you can send and receive in one interaction
The model's electricity cost only
The number of languages supported
questions.explanation: The token limit constrains the combined size of input and output text in a single interaction.

questions.q: Which is the best description of an LLM-powered 'agent' handling an M&E task?
options: It only answers one question and stops
It can plan steps, call tools (like search or a spreadsheet), and iterate toward a goal
It merely rephrases the user's question
It stores no information between steps by design
questions.explanation: An agent orchestrates multi-step work, invoking tools and iterating, rather than giving a single conversational reply.

questions.q: Why is human-in-the-loop review recommended when using LLMs for evaluation reporting?
options: Because LLMs are always wrong
Because LLMs can err or hallucinate, and accountability requires human judgment
Because it makes the model run faster
Because regulations forbid any AI use
questions.explanation: Human review catches errors and hallucinations and preserves accountability for decisions and findings.

questions.q: What is 'bias' in the context of LLM outputs?
options: A hardware defect in the server
Systematic skew in outputs reflecting patterns in the training data
The temperature being too high
A type of embedding error only
questions.explanation: LLMs can reflect and amplify biases present in their training data, which matters for equity-sensitive M&E work.

questions.q: For M&E in South Asia, why is caution needed with LLMs on low-resource local languages?
options: They always translate perfectly
Performance can be weaker due to less training data in those languages
They refuse non-English input
Local languages have no tokens
questions.explanation: Many models have less training data in low-resource languages, so quality can be lower and errors more likely.

questions.q: Which best explains why the same LLM might answer a factual question correctly once and incorrectly another time?
options: The model is deliberately deceiving the user
Sampling randomness and prediction-based generation can yield inconsistent outputs
The internet rewrote the answer
The user changed their password
questions.explanation: Probabilistic sampling means the model can generate different, sometimes inconsistent, outputs across runs.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a 'system prompt' or system instruction?
options: To set the model's role, rules, and behavior for the conversation
To display system error logs
To measure the server temperature
To count the number of tokens used
questions.explanation: A system prompt establishes the model's persona, constraints, and guidelines for how it should respond.

questions.q: An evaluation officer notices an LLM confidently states a statistic that turns out to be fabricated. The best immediate response is to:
options: Publish the statistic since the AI sounded certain
Treat it as a hallucination and verify against primary data before use
Increase the temperature and ask again
Assume all future answers are also fabricated and stop using AI entirely
questions.explanation: Unverified figures from an LLM should be checked against primary sources before being used in reporting.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT something an LLM inherently does?
options: Predict likely next tokens
Generate fluent text from a prompt
Guarantee that every factual claim it makes is true
Continue text based on learned patterns
questions.explanation: LLMs predict and generate plausible text but do not guarantee factual truth, so verification is required.

questions.q: When integrating an LLM into an M&E workflow, which combination best balances usefulness and reliability?
options: Use RAG for grounding, keep temperature low for factual tasks, and add human review
Maximize temperature and skip all review
Rely solely on the model's memory with no sources
Never verify outputs to save time
questions.explanation: Grounding with RAG, low temperature for factual work, and human review together improve accuracy and accountability.

questions.q: An M&E officer wants to use an LLM to transcribe 40 hours of recorded focus group discussions in Nepali. What is the most important quality-assurance step before trusting the transcripts?
options: Human review of a sample of transcripts against the original audio
Running the audio through the model a second time
Deleting the original audio to save storage
Assuming accuracy because the model is state-of-the-art
questions.explanation: AI transcription errors (especially in low-resource languages and with accents or overlapping speech) require human verification against source audio before the transcripts are used.

questions.q: Why is AI transcription of South Asian language interviews often less reliable than English transcription?
options: South Asian languages are grammatically simpler
Models are typically trained on far less audio data for these languages
Audio recorders work differently in South Asia
Translation is always required first
questions.explanation: Low-resource languages have much less training data, so speech-recognition accuracy is generally lower and requires more human correction.

questions.q: An evaluator asks an LLM to 'pull out the three most powerful quotes' from an interview transcript. The model returns a moving quote that does not appear in the transcript. This is an example of:
options: A fabricated (hallucinated) quote
A translation artifact
A coding error
A sampling bias
questions.explanation: LLMs can generate plausible-sounding text that was never in the source, so any quote must be verified against the actual transcript before use.

questions.q: What is the safest way to use an LLM to identify verbatim quotes from qualitative data?
options: Ask it to paraphrase the best parts
Trust whatever it returns as long as it sounds authentic
Have it point to locations, then verify each quote against the source text
Use only quotes that are emotionally compelling
questions.explanation: Because LLMs can fabricate or subtly alter wording, every quote must be checked character-for-character against the original transcript.

questions.q: When using an LLM to apply a codebook to interview transcripts, what does 'human-in-the-loop' verification primarily protect against?
options: Slow processing speeds
Miscoding and loss of contextual nuance that the model may miss
High API costs
Data storage limits
questions.explanation: Human review catches codes the model applies incorrectly and preserves contextual meaning that automated coding can flatten.

questions.q: An audit trail for AI-assisted qualitative coding should record:
options: Only the final themes
The prompts used, model version, dates, and human edits made
Just the number of transcripts processed
The evaluator's personal opinion of the tool
questions.explanation: A reproducible audit trail documents prompts, model versions, timestamps, and human corrections so the analysis can be reviewed and defended.

questions.q: AI-assisted thematic analysis is MOST trustworthy when:
options: The evaluator has no prior knowledge of the topic
AI output is treated as final without review
AI generates candidate themes that humans then validate against the data
The dataset is too large for any human to read
questions.explanation: AI works best as a first-pass idea generator whose themes are then checked and refined by an analyst who knows the context.

questions.q: A key risk of asking an LLM to 'summarise' 30 interviews into key findings is that:
options: It cannot process more than one interview
Minority or dissenting voices may be averaged out and lost
It will refuse to summarise
Summaries are always longer than the originals
questions.explanation: Summarisation tends to emphasise dominant patterns and can erase outlier perspectives that are often the most important findings.

questions.q: Which situation makes AI qualitative coding LEAST trustworthy?
options: Coding sentiment in short, clear English survey comments
Coding culturally-specific, context-heavy narratives in a low-resource language
Applying a simple binary code with clear definitions
Flagging obvious keywords for later human review
questions.explanation: Context-dependent meaning in under-resourced languages is exactly where models make the most errors and lose nuance.

questions.q: Before sending interview transcripts containing personal details to a commercial LLM API, an M&E team should first:
options: Translate them to English
Ensure informed consent and data-protection rules permit it, and de-identify where possible
Increase the model temperature
Delete the codebook
questions.explanation: Sending respondent data to third-party services raises confidentiality and consent obligations that must be checked and mitigated, e.g. by anonymising.

questions.q: What does 'inter-coder reliability' mean when validating AI-assisted coding?
options: How fast the AI codes data
The degree of agreement between coders (including AI vs. human) applying the same codes
The number of codes in the codebook
The cost per transcript
questions.explanation: Inter-coder reliability measures agreement between different coders on the same data; comparing AI codes to human codes is a way to gauge trustworthiness.

questions.q: An LLM translates a Bengali interview and renders an idiom literally, losing its meaning. The best response is to:
options: Publish the literal translation as-is
Have a bilingual analyst review and correct culturally-loaded passages
Assume the idiom was unimportant
Re-run the translation at a higher temperature
questions.explanation: Machine translation frequently mishandles idioms and cultural expressions, so bilingual human review is essential for meaning-critical passages.

questions.q: Why should the exact prompt used to code qualitative data be saved as part of the analysis record?
options: Prompts are copyrighted
Different prompts produce different codes, so reproducibility and transparency require documenting them
It reduces the API cost
The model needs the prompt again to decode
questions.explanation: Prompt wording strongly shapes output; saving prompts makes the coding process transparent and reproducible.

questions.q: A funder asks how you ensured AI-generated themes reflect what respondents actually said. The strongest evidence is:
options: The model's reputation
A documented process of human validation, quote-checking, and an audit trail
The speed of the analysis
The number of themes produced
questions.explanation: Credibility rests on demonstrable human verification and a traceable audit trail, not on the tool's brand or output volume.

questions.q: Which of these is a legitimate strength of using LLMs in qualitative analysis?
options: Eliminating the need for human judgement
Rapidly generating a first-pass structure across large volumes of text
Guaranteeing unbiased results
Producing quotes that never need checking
questions.explanation: LLMs can quickly organise and surface patterns in large text corpora as a starting point for human-led analysis, but they do not remove the need for judgement or verification.

questions.q: 'Confirmation bias' can enter AI-assisted analysis when:
options: The evaluator prompts the model to find evidence for a conclusion they already hold
The model runs out of tokens
The transcripts are too short
The audio quality is poor
questions.explanation: Leading prompts push the model to surface supporting evidence and ignore disconfirming data, reinforcing the analyst's prior beliefs.

questions.q: To reduce the chance that an LLM invents themes not grounded in the data, a good practice is to:
options: Ask it to be creative
Require it to cite specific transcript excerpts for every theme it proposes
Increase the temperature setting
Give it no examples
questions.explanation: Requiring grounded citations forces themes to be traceable to real text and makes fabrication easy to detect.

questions.q: An M&E team uses AI to code 500 open-ended survey responses. Which validation approach is most defensible?
options: Manually double-code a random sample and measure agreement with the AI
Trust the AI fully because the sample is large
Only review responses the AI flagged as positive
Skip validation to save time
questions.explanation: Double-coding a random sample and measuring AI-human agreement gives a quantified, defensible estimate of coding quality.

questions.q: Why is model 'temperature' relevant when using LLMs for coding qualitative data?
options: Higher temperature guarantees accuracy
Lower temperature yields more consistent, deterministic outputs suited to structured coding
Temperature controls the language of output
Temperature only affects translation
questions.explanation: Lower temperature reduces randomness, giving more consistent and reproducible coding, which is desirable for structured tasks.

questions.q: A major limitation of AI summaries of FGDs for accountability reporting is that they:
options: Are always too short to be useful
May smooth over disagreement and present false consensus
Cannot be edited by humans
Require no source data
questions.explanation: Summarisation can manufacture an impression of consensus and hide the very disagreements evaluators need to report.

questions.q: When is it acceptable to skip human review of AI-transcribed audio entirely?
options: When the recording is in a low-resource language
When accuracy is safety- or decision-critical
Rarely: for informal, low-stakes internal notes it may be acceptable, but decision-critical use always needs review
Whenever the model claims high confidence
questions.explanation: Only very low-stakes uses might skip review; any transcript feeding decisions, quotes, or reporting requires human verification.

questions.q: The main reason to de-identify transcripts before AI processing is to:
options: Improve model accuracy
Protect respondent confidentiality and reduce data-protection risk
Make files smaller
Speed up transcription
questions.explanation: Removing names and identifying details protects participants and helps meet ethical and legal data-protection obligations.

questions.q: An LLM confidently assigns a theme of 'economic empowerment' to a passage that is actually about social stigma. This illustrates that AI coding:
options: Is always correct
Can be confidently wrong, requiring human validation
Only fails on long transcripts
Cannot assign themes at all
questions.explanation: Models produce confident output even when wrong, so apparent confidence is not evidence of correctness and human checking is needed.

questions.q: Which practice best supports reproducibility of an AI-assisted qualitative analysis?
options: Using a different model each run
Recording the model name/version, prompts, parameters, and processing dates
Deleting intermediate outputs
Paraphrasing prompts differently each time
questions.explanation: Documenting model version, prompts, parameters and dates allows the analysis to be repeated and audited.

questions.q: A risk specific to using LLMs for cross-language qualitative work is:
options: Translation may introduce errors that then propagate into coding and themes
Models cannot read non-English text
Translation is always perfect
Coding is unaffected by translation
questions.explanation: Errors in machine translation carry forward into every downstream step, so translation quality must be verified before coding.

questions.q: To keep an audit trail useful, AI-assisted coding outputs should be stored:
options: Only in the analyst's memory
Alongside the source excerpts they were derived from
Without any link to source data
As screenshots only
questions.explanation: Linking each code or theme to its source excerpt lets reviewers trace and verify how conclusions were reached.

questions.q: An evaluator notices the AI consistently under-codes responses from women in a mixed dataset. This most likely reflects:
options: A random glitch
Bias in the model or prompt that must be investigated and corrected
Correct behaviour
A transcription speed issue
questions.explanation: Systematic under-coding of a subgroup signals bias that could distort findings and must be examined and addressed.

questions.q: Which is the best framing of AI's role in qualitative analysis for a rigorous evaluation?
options: A replacement for the qualitative analyst
An assistant that accelerates analysis under human direction and verification
An unbiased oracle of truth
A tool that removes the need for a codebook
questions.explanation: AI augments but does not replace the analyst; human direction, judgement, and verification remain central.

questions.q: A team wants AI to deductively code transcripts using an existing codebook. What should the prompt include for best results?
options: Only the transcripts
The codebook definitions with clear examples for each code
The evaluator's conclusions
Nothing: let the model decide
questions.explanation: Providing explicit code definitions and examples grounds the model in the intended scheme and improves consistency.

questions.q: Why is it risky to let an LLM both generate themes and then declare which are 'most important'?
options: It cannot count
Importance judgements need program context and stakeholder values the model lacks
It will always pick the first theme
Themes cannot be ranked
questions.explanation: Prioritising findings requires contextual and normative judgement about what matters to the program and stakeholders, which humans must provide.

questions.q: What is a sound way to test whether an AI coding approach is trustworthy before scaling it?
options: Pilot it on a subset already coded by humans and compare
Apply it to all data immediately
Ask the model if it is accurate
Use it only on the largest transcripts
questions.explanation: Benchmarking AI output against a human-coded gold-standard subset reveals accuracy and error patterns before full deployment.

questions.q: An LLM's tendency to produce fluent, well-structured summaries can be dangerous because:
options: Fluency can mask inaccuracy and lend false credibility
Summaries are illegible
It slows down reading
Structure is never useful
questions.explanation: Polished, confident writing can make inaccurate or fabricated content seem authoritative, so fluency should not be mistaken for accuracy.

questions.q: When documenting AI use in an evaluation report, transparency requires disclosing:
options: Nothing, to avoid criticism
Which tasks used AI, the model, and how outputs were verified
Only the positive results
Just the tool's marketing name
questions.explanation: Ethical reporting discloses where AI was used, the model, and the verification steps so readers can judge reliability.

questions.q: A practical safeguard against fabricated quotes is to:
options: Trust the model's formatting
Use exact-match search to confirm each quoted string exists in the source transcript
Ask the model to rate its own honesty
Only use very short quotes
questions.explanation: An automated exact-string search against the source verifies that quoted text is genuine and not invented.

questions.q: Inductive (open) coding with an LLM is most appropriate when the evaluator:
options: Wants to enforce a fixed codebook exactly
Is exploring data to surface emergent themes, then curates them
Has no data
Wants to avoid reading any transcripts
questions.explanation: LLMs can suggest emergent codes in exploratory work, but the analyst must curate and validate what surfaces.

questions.q: Why keep the original audio and transcripts even after AI analysis is complete?
options: To retrain the model
So findings can be traced back and verified against primary sources
Audio files are decorative
It is required to delete them
questions.explanation: Retaining primary sources preserves the audit trail so any AI-derived claim can be checked against original data.

questions.q: An LLM given a very long transcript may 'lose' content in the middle. This limitation is related to:
options: Context-window and attention limitations
The language of the transcript
The interviewer's tone
The file format
questions.explanation: Long inputs can exceed effective context handling, causing the model to under-weight or omit middle content, so chunking and checks are needed.

questions.q: For sensitive topics (e.g. gender-based violence testimony), the strongest reason to limit AI use is:
options: AI is too fast
Confidentiality risks and the harm of misrepresenting survivor accounts
AI cannot read the text
It costs too much
questions.explanation: Highly sensitive testimony carries serious confidentiality and dignity risks if mishandled or distorted by automated tools.

questions.q: Which statement about AI and researcher reflexivity is correct?
options: AI removes the need for reflexivity
AI can obscure the analyst's positionality, so reflexivity remains essential
Reflexivity is only for quantitative work
AI is inherently reflexive
questions.explanation: Automation can hide the interpretive choices being made, so analysts must stay reflexive about how AI shapes findings.

questions.q: A good chunking strategy when coding long transcripts with an LLM is to:
options: Split arbitrarily mid-sentence
Split at natural boundaries (e.g. by speaker turn or question) to preserve context
Never split, regardless of length
Combine all transcripts into one block
questions.explanation: Splitting at meaningful boundaries keeps context intact within each chunk and reduces coding errors.

questions.q: If two runs of the same prompt on the same transcript give different codes, the evaluator should:
options: Pick whichever they prefer
Treat the instability as a reliability concern and add human adjudication or lower temperature
Ignore it
Assume both are equally correct and average them silently
questions.explanation: Output instability signals unreliability that must be addressed through human adjudication and settings that increase consistency.

questions.q: The primary purpose of a 'gold standard' human-coded sample in AI-assisted analysis is to:
options: Train the evaluator
Provide a benchmark to measure and monitor AI coding accuracy
Replace the codebook
Increase the dataset size
questions.explanation: A gold-standard sample is the reference against which AI accuracy is measured and tracked over time.

questions.q: Which is a responsible disclosure to participants when AI will process their interview data?
options: No disclosure is ever needed
Informing them in consent that AI tools may be used and how data is protected
Telling them only after publication
Disclosing only to funders
questions.explanation: Informed consent should cover the use of AI tools and the safeguards protecting participants' data.

questions.q: An LLM summary states '80% of participants felt empowered', but participants were never asked a yes/no empowerment question. This is a case of:
options: Valid quantification
AI inventing false precision from qualitative data
Correct triangulation
Proper coding
questions.explanation: Attaching invented statistics to open-ended qualitative data manufactures false precision and misrepresents the evidence.

questions.q: To preserve nuance when AI summarises diverse views, an evaluator should:
options: Ask only for the majority view
Explicitly prompt for divergent, minority, and contradictory perspectives
Discard outliers
Summarise only the shortest responses
questions.explanation: Prompting the model to surface disagreement and minority views counteracts summarisation's tendency to flatten diversity.

questions.q: Why is it important that a human, not the AI, makes the final interpretation of findings?
options: Humans type faster
Interpretation requires accountability, context, and ethical judgement AI cannot own
AI refuses to interpret
Humans are always unbiased
questions.explanation: Final interpretation carries accountability and demands contextual and ethical judgement that must rest with a person.

questions.q: A defensible way to combine AI and human effort in coding is:
options: AI codes everything, humans check nothing
AI does a first pass, humans review, correct, and resolve ambiguous cases
Humans code, then delete their work
AI and humans work without any comparison
questions.explanation: An AI-first-pass with systematic human review and adjudication balances efficiency with rigour.

questions.q: Which factor most increases the trustworthiness of AI-assisted qualitative coding?
options: A larger model alone
Clear code definitions, human validation, and a documented audit trail
Faster hardware
A more expensive API plan
questions.explanation: Trustworthiness comes from good definitions, human validation, and traceability, not from model size or cost.

questions.q: An evaluator should be MOST cautious about AI output when:
options: The stakes of the decision are low
Findings will directly shape funding or program-continuation decisions
The data is already public
The transcript is in fluent English
questions.explanation: High-stakes decisions demand the most rigorous human verification of any AI-derived findings.

questions.q: What is a correct statement about bias in LLM qualitative analysis?
options: LLMs are free of bias
LLMs can reflect biases in training data and prompts, requiring active mitigation
Bias only affects images
Bias disappears with more data automatically
questions.explanation: Models inherit biases from training data and prompt framing, so bias must be actively checked and mitigated, not assumed absent.

questions.q: An M&E officer asks an AI chatbot to write Python code to clean a survey dataset. What is the safest first step before trusting the output?
options: Run the code on the full production dataset immediately
Read the code line by line and test it on a small sample to confirm it does what is intended
Assume it is correct because AI rarely makes coding mistakes
Delete the original data so only the cleaned version remains
questions.explanation: AI-generated code can contain silent errors, so reviewing it and testing on a sample before full use protects data integrity.

questions.q: You ask an AI to summarize the average household income from a dataset it cannot actually see. It returns a specific figure like '₹42,350'. This is most likely an example of:
options: A verified calculation
A confidence interval
A weighted mean
A hallucinated (made-up) number
questions.explanation: When an AI has no access to the actual data, any precise numeric result is fabricated and must never be reported as real.

questions.q: Which practice best supports reproducibility of an AI-assisted analysis?
options: Keeping the analysis only in the chat window
Relying on memory of what steps were taken
Regenerating the analysis freshly each time with new prompts
Saving the exact prompts, code, data version, and random seeds used
questions.explanation: Recording prompts, code, data versions, and seeds lets others (and your future self) reproduce the same results.

questions.q: An AI writes SQL that returns a suspiciously small number of rows from your indicator table. What should you do first?
options: Publish the result since the query ran without errors
Assume the database is missing data
Rewrite the entire database schema
Inspect the WHERE and JOIN clauses for filters that may silently drop rows
questions.explanation: A query that runs successfully can still be logically wrong, so checking JOIN and filter conditions catches silent data loss.

questions.q: Why is 'human-in-the-loop' important when using AI for data analysis in M&E?
options: A person validates outputs, catches errors, and takes accountability for decisions
It slows the work down for compliance reasons only
It lets the AI make final programmatic decisions faster
It is only needed for qualitative data
questions.explanation: Human oversight ensures errors and biases are caught and that a person remains accountable for conclusions drawn.

questions.q: An AI cleans your data by 'dropping all rows with any missing value.' What is the main risk?
options: The file becomes larger
You may lose a large, non-random portion of respondents and bias results
The column names change
The data becomes encrypted
questions.explanation: Listwise deletion can remove many cases and introduce bias if missingness is related to the outcomes being studied.

questions.q: You want AI to explain an unfamiliar block of R code inherited from a colleague. This use of AI is:
options: Unreliable and should never be attempted
A violation of data privacy by default
A reasonable use, though you should still verify the explanation against the code's behavior
Only valid for Python, not R
questions.explanation: AI is good at explaining code, but you should confirm the explanation matches what the code actually does when run.

questions.q: Which is a 'silent error' in AI-generated data code?
options: A syntax error that stops the program
Code that runs successfully but computes the wrong result, e.g. summing instead of averaging
A missing import that raises an exception
A typo in a comment
questions.explanation: Silent errors are dangerous precisely because the code runs without complaint while producing incorrect numbers.

questions.q: An AI generates a bar chart from your program data. Before sharing it, you should first check that:
options: The chart uses attractive colors
The axis labels, units, scale, and totals match the underlying data
The chart has a 3D effect
The file size is small
questions.explanation: Visual polish is irrelevant if the axes, units, or aggregations misrepresent the actual data.

questions.q: When pasting sensitive beneficiary data into a public AI tool to clean it, the primary concern is:
options: Data privacy and potential exposure of personally identifiable information
The AI will format it incorrectly
The AI will run out of memory
Charts will render slowly
questions.explanation: Sharing identifiable data with third-party tools can breach privacy commitments and data protection norms.

questions.q: An AI reports a correlation of 0.9 between two indicators from your data. The best interpretation is:
options: The two indicators cause each other
The analysis is definitely wrong
One indicator must be deleted
There is a strong linear association, but causation is not established
questions.explanation: Correlation measures association strength, not causation, which requires additional design and evidence.

questions.q: To reduce hallucinated numbers when using AI on real data, the best approach is to:
options: Ask the AI to guess the numbers confidently
Have the AI write code you run yourself, so numbers come from actual computation
Trust any figure the AI states in prose
Use a longer prompt with more adjectives
questions.explanation: Letting AI produce code you execute means the numbers come from the data, not from the model's text generation.

questions.q: An AI suggests using the mean to fill missing income values (mean imputation). A key downside is that it:
options: Artificially reduces variance and can distort relationships
Always increases the sample size
Makes the data categorical
Corrupts the column headers
questions.explanation: Mean imputation understates variability and can weaken or bias correlations and standard errors.

questions.q: What does 'exploratory data analysis' (EDA) with AI typically involve?
options: Finalizing conclusions without looking at distributions
Only producing the final report
Encrypting the dataset
Summarizing distributions, spotting patterns, outliers, and data quality issues before formal analysis
questions.explanation: EDA is about understanding the data's shape, quality, and patterns before committing to formal models.

questions.q: An AI flags several data points as anomalies. The correct M&E response is to:
options: Automatically delete them all
Ignore the flag entirely
Report them as fraud
Investigate whether they are genuine errors, valid extremes, or data entry mistakes
questions.explanation: Anomalies can be real, erroneous, or meaningful outliers, so each needs investigation before action.

questions.q: Why should you specify the exact column names and data types when asking AI to write cleaning code?
options: It makes the prompt longer
It hides the data from the AI
It reduces the chance the AI guesses wrong structures and writes code that fails or mismatches
It changes the file format
questions.explanation: Giving accurate schema details helps the AI produce code that matches your real dataset structure.

questions.q: An AI writes code using a library function that does not exist. This is an example of:
options: A valid optimization
A caching strategy
A hallucinated API/function that will fail or must be corrected
A reproducibility feature
questions.explanation: AI can invent plausible-sounding functions that do not exist, so imports and function names must be verified.

questions.q: The most robust way to validate an AI-produced summary statistic is to:
options: Independently recompute it using a tool or method you trust
Ask the same AI if it is sure
Check the grammar of the explanation
Assume it is right if it sounds precise
questions.explanation: Independent recomputation, not self-confirmation by the model, is what actually verifies a result.

questions.q: When AI generates a chart, a common misleading practice to watch for is:
options: Using a clearly labeled y-axis starting at zero
Including a legend
Adding a descriptive title
A truncated y-axis that exaggerates small differences
questions.explanation: Non-zero or truncated axes can visually exaggerate differences and mislead the audience.

questions.q: You give AI a messy date column with mixed formats. A safe cleaning approach is to:
options: Have AI standardize formats but review a sample to confirm no dates were misparsed
Let AI silently overwrite all dates
Delete the date column
Convert all dates to today's date
questions.explanation: Mixed date formats are easily misparsed, so spot-checking converted values prevents silent corruption.

questions.q: For an M&E dashboard, why keep the AI-generated code rather than just the final numbers?
options: Code files look more professional
To increase storage costs
Because numbers cannot be trusted at all
So the analysis can be re-run, audited, and updated when new data arrives
questions.explanation: Retaining code makes the pipeline auditable and re-runnable as data updates, supporting reproducibility.

questions.q: An AI proposes removing 'outlier' beneficiaries with very high program costs. Before doing so you should:
options: Remove them without checking
Double the values instead
Understand why the values are high, as they may be legitimate and important cases
Hide them from the report
questions.explanation: High-cost cases may reflect real, policy-relevant situations, so removal must be justified, not automatic.

questions.q: What is a good prompt technique to get more reliable AI data code?
options: Ask for the answer with no explanation
Ask the AI to add comments and print intermediate results so you can check each step
Request the shortest possible code
Forbid the AI from showing its work
questions.explanation: Comments and intermediate outputs make the logic transparent and easier to verify step by step.

questions.q: An AI computes a percentage change and the denominator is zero in some rows. A reliable analysis should:
options: Handle division-by-zero explicitly and flag those rows for review
Report 'infinity' as a finding
Delete the whole dataset
Ignore the issue
questions.explanation: Division-by-zero must be handled deliberately, or it produces misleading or invalid results.

questions.q: Why is it risky to let AI 'auto-detect' the delimiter and encoding of a raw CSV without checking?
options: It always works perfectly
Misdetection can silently shift columns or corrupt characters, especially with non-Latin scripts
It changes the operating system
It deletes the header row by design
questions.explanation: Wrong delimiter or encoding detection can misalign columns and garble text such as Hindi or Bangla characters.

questions.q: The main reason to test AI-generated code on a known example with a known answer is to:
options: Make the code slower
Avoid writing documentation
Confirm the code produces the correct expected result before using it on real data
Increase the dataset size
questions.explanation: Validating against a known answer is a direct check that the code logic is correct.

questions.q: An AI describes a trend as 'statistically significant' from your data summary. You should treat this claim as:
options: Needing verification of the actual test, sample size, and assumptions
Automatically true
Irrelevant to M&E
Proof of program impact
questions.explanation: Significance claims depend on the underlying test and assumptions, which must be checked rather than assumed.

questions.q: When AI joins two datasets on a common ID, duplicate IDs can cause:
options: Row multiplication (a many-to-many join) that inflates counts
Perfectly clean output always
Automatic deduplication
Encryption of the result
questions.explanation: Duplicate keys in a join can multiply rows and inflate totals, a common silent error to check for.

questions.q: A defensible way to document an AI-assisted cleaning pipeline is to:
options: Keep it entirely in your head
Rename files randomly
Write a data dictionary and log of each transformation applied
Delete intermediate files immediately
questions.explanation: A transformation log and data dictionary make the pipeline transparent and reproducible.

questions.q: An AI chart shows program reach rising sharply, but the last data point is a partial month. The honest fix is to:
options: Leave it to look impressive
Multiply the partial month by ten
Annotate or exclude the incomplete period so the trend is not misread
Remove the axis labels
questions.explanation: Incomplete final periods should be flagged or excluded to avoid a misleading apparent trend.

questions.q: Which statement about AI and reproducibility is most accurate?
options: AI outputs are always identical for the same prompt
Reproducibility is impossible with any AI
AI text responses can vary run to run, so pinning code and data is what ensures reproducible results
Reproducibility only matters for qualitative work
questions.explanation: Generative models can give different phrasings each run, so the reproducible artifact is the code and data, not the chat.

questions.q: You ask AI to 'fix all the errors' in a large dataset. The safest interpretation is that AI should:
options: Flag suspected issues for your review rather than auto-editing real data
Silently change values it thinks are wrong
Delete the dataset and start over
Encrypt every field
questions.explanation: Automated 'fixing' of data risks introducing errors, so flagging for human review is safer than silent edits.

questions.q: A key benefit of asking AI to write R or Python instead of doing the math in chat is that:
options: Executable code is testable, reproducible, and computes on the real data
Chat math is always more accurate
Code cannot be shared
It avoids all errors permanently
questions.explanation: Running code on data is verifiable and reproducible, unlike arithmetic the model performs in prose.

questions.q: An AI recommends a complex machine-learning model for a small M&E dataset. A sensible caution is:
options: With small samples, simpler methods may be more reliable and interpretable
Complex models are always better
Sample size never matters
You must use the most advanced model available
questions.explanation: Complex models can overfit small datasets; simpler, interpretable methods are often more trustworthy.

questions.q: When validating an AI-produced number, comparing it against a known total or 'sanity check' (e.g., it cannot exceed the sample size) helps catch:
options: Font problems
Logically impossible results indicating a code or data error
Slow internet
Color-blindness issues
questions.explanation: Sanity checks against logical bounds quickly reveal impossible values caused by bugs.

questions.q: Why should M&E teams avoid copy-pasting AI code they do not understand into production pipelines?
options: It always crashes
Unreviewed code can contain hidden errors or unsafe operations affecting real decisions
It is illegal everywhere
It cannot be edited later
questions.explanation: Understanding the code is essential because unreviewed logic may silently corrupt data or conclusions.

questions.q: An AI produces a pivot table that double-counts beneficiaries served in multiple months. The root issue is:
options: Chart color choice
Font size
File encoding
Aggregation logic not deduplicating unique individuals
questions.explanation: Counting the same person across periods inflates unique-reach figures unless deduplicated by ID.

questions.q: Which is the best description of using AI to 'explain what this error message means'?
options: A misuse of AI
Guaranteed to solve the bug instantly
A helpful debugging aid, though the suggested fix should still be tested
Only valid for SQL
questions.explanation: AI can interpret error messages well, but proposed fixes must be verified by running the corrected code.

questions.q: To keep an AI-assisted analysis auditable for a donor review, you should retain:
options: Only the final PDF
Just the chart images
Nothing, to save space
The raw data, cleaning code, prompts, and a record of decisions made
questions.explanation: An audit trail of raw data, code, prompts, and decisions lets reviewers trace how results were produced.

questions.q: An AI standardizes district names but merges two genuinely different districts with similar spellings. This shows that:
options: Fuzzy matching is always safe
Automated text matching can create false merges that need human verification
District names never vary
AI cannot process text
questions.explanation: Fuzzy name matching can incorrectly merge distinct entities, so results require human confirmation.

questions.q: The phrase 'garbage in, garbage out' in AI-assisted analysis means:
options: AI improves poor-quality data automatically
If the input data is flawed, the AI's outputs and charts will also be flawed
Only output matters
Data quality is irrelevant with AI
questions.explanation: AI cannot rescue fundamentally bad data; poor inputs yield unreliable outputs regardless of the tool.

questions.q: A good reason to ask an AI to show the code's assumptions (e.g., 'assumes no negative values') is that:
