options: It lengthens the response unnecessarily
It hides the logic
It surfaces conditions that, if violated in your data, would make results wrong
It prevents reproducibility
questions.explanation: Surfacing assumptions lets you check whether they hold in your actual data before trusting the output.

questions.q: When an AI writes code to compute an indicator, versioning that code in a repository primarily helps with:
options: Making the code run faster
Hiding it from colleagues
Tracking changes over time and reproducing past results
Reducing data quality
questions.explanation: Version control records how analysis evolved and lets you reproduce results from any prior point.

questions.q: An AI summary says 'the program reduced dropout rates by 30%,' but your data only covers enrollment, not dropout. This is a sign of:
options: A fabricated or unsupported claim not grounded in the available data
A valid finding
A statistical adjustment
A reproducible result
questions.explanation: Claims about variables not present in the data are unsupported and likely hallucinated.

questions.q: Which approach best balances AI efficiency with rigor in M&E analysis?
options: Let AI produce and publish results with no review
Avoid AI entirely
Use AI to draft code and analysis, then have a human verify, test, and sign off
Only trust AI for final decisions
questions.explanation: Combining AI drafting with human verification captures efficiency gains while preserving accountability and accuracy.

questions.q: An AI-generated scatter plot omits 200 rows with missing values without saying so. The risk is that:
options: The chart is more accurate
The file becomes corrupt
The axes disappear
Viewers assume all data is shown, leading to misinterpretation
questions.explanation: Silently dropped data can mislead viewers into thinking the chart represents the complete dataset.

questions.q: Before using AI to recode open-ended survey responses into categories, a prudent step is to:
options: Accept all codes without review
Manually check a sample of AI codings for accuracy and consistency
Delete responses that are hard to code
Assume 100% accuracy
questions.explanation: Spot-checking AI-assigned codes against human judgment ensures the categorization is reliable.

questions.q: Why is it good practice to ask AI to compute a result two different ways?
options: To waste time
Agreement between independent methods increases confidence the result is correct
To make the code longer
To confuse reviewers
questions.explanation: Cross-checking with a second method is a practical way to catch errors in either approach.

questions.q: An AI cleaning script converts a text ID column to numbers, dropping leading zeros (e.g., '007' becomes 7). This can cause:
options: Faster processing only
Better data quality
Automatic backups
Broken joins and mismatched records when IDs no longer match
questions.explanation: Coercing identifier strings to numbers loses leading zeros and breaks matches with the original keys.

questions.q: The overarching principle for using AI in quantitative M&E work is best summarized as:
options: Treat AI as a fast assistant whose work you verify, document, and remain accountable for
Trust the AI output by default
Replace analysts with AI entirely
Never check any AI output
questions.explanation: AI accelerates analysis, but human verification, documentation, and accountability remain essential.

questions.q: In prompt engineering, why is giving a large language model a clear, specific instruction more effective than a vague one for M&E tasks?
options: Vague prompts cause the model to refuse to answer entirely
Vague instructions force the model to guess your intent, increasing the chance of irrelevant or generic output
Specific instructions make the model run faster on the server
Clear instructions reduce the cost of API tokens by half
questions.explanation: Specificity anchors the model to your actual goal, so it produces targeted output instead of guessing among many plausible interpretations.

questions.q: An M&E officer wants an AI to summarise a field report. Which instruction is most likely to yield a usable result?
options: Summarise this report
Make it shorter
Tell me about this document
Summarise this in three bullet points focused on outcomes for adolescent girls, each under 20 words
questions.explanation: The first specifies length, focus, and format, giving the model concrete constraints that produce a predictable, relevant summary.

questions.q: What does 'few-shot prompting' mean in the context of drafting M&E indicators?
options: Asking the model only a few questions per session
Providing the model with a few worked examples of good indicators before asking it to write new ones
Limiting the prompt to a few words
Running the prompt only a few times before accepting any answer
questions.explanation: Few-shot prompting supplies example input-output pairs so the model can infer the pattern and style you want it to follow.

questions.q: Providing context such as the project's sector, target population, and donor framework in a prompt primarily helps the model to:
options: Reduce the total number of words it generates
Bypass its safety filters
Translate the output automatically
Ground its output in your specific programme rather than generic development jargon
questions.explanation: Context narrows the model's assumptions so responses reflect your programme's realities instead of default generalities.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of 'role prompting' for an M&E workflow?
options: Write 500 words
You are an experienced monitoring and evaluation specialist reviewing a logframe for a WASH project
Please answer quickly and accurately
Do not make mistakes
questions.explanation: Role prompting assigns the model a persona or expertise frame, which shapes tone, vocabulary, and depth toward that role.

questions.q: When you ask a model to return output as a JSON object with fixed keys like indicator, baseline, and target, you are using:
options: Zero-shot prompting
Adversarial prompting
Structured output prompting
Chain-of-thought prompting
questions.explanation: Requesting a specific schema (JSON, table, fixed fields) is structured output prompting, which makes results easier to parse and reuse.

questions.q: At a concept level, 'chain-of-thought' prompting encourages the model to:
options: Reason through intermediate steps before giving a final answer
Cite academic sources for every claim
Repeat the question back to you
Chain multiple API calls together automatically
questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought asks the model to show or work through intermediate reasoning, which often improves accuracy on multi-step tasks.

questions.q: Why might chain-of-thought reasoning improve an AI's help in classifying qualitative interview responses?
options: It makes the model ignore the interview text
It automatically anonymises the respondents
It guarantees the model will never be wrong
Breaking the judgement into steps reduces snap misclassifications and surfaces the model's rationale
questions.explanation: Stepwise reasoning lets the model weigh evidence before deciding, and the visible rationale helps you catch errors.

questions.q: 'Iterating on prompts' in an M&E workflow most accurately describes:
options: Sending the same prompt repeatedly until you get lucky
Using a loop in code to call the API
Asking the model to iterate over a dataset
Refining the prompt across attempts based on what the model got wrong or missed
questions.explanation: Iteration is the deliberate practice of improving your wording, examples, and constraints after examining each output's shortcomings.

questions.q: Which is the strongest safeguard against an AI hallucinating statistics in a draft evaluation report?
options: Ask it to sound confident
Set the temperature to maximum
Use a longer prompt
Instruct the model to use only the figures you provide and to flag any it cannot verify
questions.explanation: Constraining the model to supplied data and asking it to flag uncertainty directly reduces fabricated numbers.

questions.q: A 'hallucination' from a language model refers to:
options: A response in the wrong language
A deliberately creative poem
A confident-sounding output that is factually wrong or fabricated
The model crashing mid-response
questions.explanation: Hallucination is plausible but false or invented content presented as if it were accurate.

questions.q: When prompting an AI to draft a Theory of Change, which framing best reduces the risk of a generic, off-the-shelf answer?
options: Provide the programme's specific problem, target group, activities, and assumptions as context
Ask for a Theory of Change in one word
Ask it to write the best possible Theory of Change
Tell it to be creative
questions.explanation: Feeding programme-specific context forces the model to build the causal logic around your actual intervention.

questions.q: Which prompt element most directly controls the FORMAT of an AI's answer?
options: Assigning it an expert role
Specifying output as a markdown table with named columns
Telling it the project's budget
Setting a friendly tone
questions.explanation: Explicit format instructions (table, columns, bullets, JSON) govern the shape of the output more than role or context.

questions.q: A key limitation of prompting alone (without external tools or data) is that the model:
options: Always refuses M&E questions
Cannot access your latest project data unless you include it in the prompt
Can never write in complete sentences
Cannot follow instructions of any kind
questions.explanation: A base model only knows its training data plus what you provide; recent or private project data must be supplied in the prompt.

questions.q: You ask an AI to 'evaluate whether this indicator is SMART.' To make the task reliable, you should also:
options: Ask it to guess
Tell it to answer yes or no only
Set no constraints at all
Define what each SMART criterion means so the model applies a consistent standard
questions.explanation: Defining the evaluation rubric gives the model an explicit standard, producing consistent, checkable judgements.

questions.q: In few-shot prompting for coding open-ended survey responses, the examples you provide should ideally:
options: Be unrelated to the survey topic
All belong to a single category
Be as long as possible regardless of relevance
Cover the range of categories the model must distinguish, including tricky edge cases
questions.explanation: Representative examples spanning categories and edge cases teach the model the decision boundaries you care about.

questions.q: Which statement about temperature or randomness settings is most accurate for M&E drafting tasks?
options: Lower randomness tends to give more consistent, deterministic output suited to factual drafting
Temperature has no effect on outputs
Randomness settings affect only the language, not the content
Higher randomness always improves accuracy
questions.explanation: Lower temperature reduces variability, which is generally preferable when you want reliable, repeatable factual output.

questions.q: A good practice when using AI to draft an evaluation report section is to:
options: Treat the draft as a starting point requiring human verification of all facts and figures
Publish it directly to the donor without review
Remove all human involvement to save time
Assume the AI has read your project documents
questions.explanation: AI drafts accelerate writing but must be fact-checked by a person, since the model can introduce errors.

questions.q: Why is it useful to ask an AI to 'explain its reasoning' when it recommends an evaluation method?
options: It forces the model to always agree with you
It makes the answer longer for no reason
The rationale lets you judge whether the recommendation is sound or based on faulty assumptions
It hides the model's uncertainty
questions.explanation: Seeing the reasoning exposes the assumptions behind a recommendation so you can validate or challenge it.

questions.q: Which prompt is most likely to produce a hallucinated citation?
options: Summarise the argument in the text I pasted below
Rewrite this paragraph more clearly
List five peer-reviewed studies proving this programme worked, with authors and years
Convert these bullet points into a table
questions.explanation: Asking a model to produce specific citations it hasn't been given invites fabricated references, a classic hallucination.

questions.q: When defining the desired OUTPUT for a prompt, the most helpful thing you can add is:
options: A concrete example of what a correct answer looks like
The word please
A very high word count
A request to be helpful
questions.explanation: A concrete target example communicates format and quality expectations more precisely than adjectives.

questions.q: An M&E team notices the AI keeps inventing sample sizes. The best first fix is to:
options: Explicitly instruct it not to invent numbers and to write 'not provided' when data is missing
Add more examples of invented numbers
Increase the temperature
Ask it to try harder
questions.explanation: A direct constraint against fabrication, with an instruction to mark gaps, curbs invented data at the source.

questions.q: Role prompting an AI as a 'skeptical evaluation reviewer' is useful because it:
options: Encourages the model to identify weaknesses and gaps rather than only praise
Guarantees the report has no errors
Removes the need for human review
Makes the model refuse the task
questions.explanation: A critical persona biases the model toward surfacing problems, which is valuable for quality assurance.

questions.q: Which of these is a limitation prompting CANNOT overcome on its own?
options: The ability to assign a role
The option to provide examples
The model's lack of knowledge about events after its training cutoff
The need to specify output format
questions.explanation: No prompt can give a model knowledge of events beyond its training cutoff unless that information is supplied in the prompt.

questions.q: When asking an AI to draft indicators for a logframe, providing the outcome statement as context helps because:
options: Longer prompts always score higher
The model cannot write without an outcome
Indicators must measure the specific outcome, so the model needs to know it precisely
It reduces the token cost
questions.explanation: Indicators are meaningless without the outcome they measure, so the outcome statement is essential context.

questions.q: 'Structured output' is especially valuable in M&E workflows when you plan to:
options: Translate the answer manually
Print the answer on paper only
Import the AI's response into a spreadsheet or database
Read the answer once and discard it
questions.explanation: Consistent structure (columns, keys) makes machine parsing and import into tools like spreadsheets straightforward.

questions.q: A prompt that says 'Act as a data protection officer and flag any personal identifiers in this dataset description' combines which two techniques?
options: Chain-of-thought and translation
Zero-shot and temperature control
Few-shot and structured output
Role prompting and a clear task instruction
questions.explanation: It assigns a persona (role prompting) and states a specific task, combining two distinct techniques.

questions.q: Why should you test a prompt on several different inputs before adopting it for routine M&E use?
options: A prompt that works on one case may fail on edge cases or different data
The model behaves identically on all inputs
One successful test proves the prompt is perfect
Testing wastes tokens and should be avoided
questions.explanation: Robustness comes from checking varied inputs, since a prompt tuned to one example can break on others.

questions.q: Which instruction best guards against an AI overstating a programme's impact in a report draft?
options: Use superlatives throughout
Ignore the evidence and be optimistic
Base all impact claims strictly on the evidence provided and note where evidence is weak
Make the impact sound as strong as possible
questions.explanation: Tying claims to provided evidence and flagging weak spots prevents inflated, unsupported impact statements.

questions.q: In prompt engineering, 'zero-shot' prompting means:
options: Asking the model to perform a task with no examples, relying on the instruction alone
Giving the model zero context
Setting the temperature to zero
Sending an empty prompt
questions.explanation: Zero-shot means no examples are provided; the model works from the instruction and its prior training.

questions.q: An M&E analyst wants consistent categorisation across 500 responses. The most reliable approach is to:
options: Change the prompt wording for each response
Let the model invent new categories each time
Provide a fixed set of category definitions and few-shot examples, then apply the same prompt to each
Use a different role for every response
questions.explanation: A fixed rubric plus examples, applied uniformly, produces consistent categorisation across many items.

questions.q: What is a realistic expectation when using AI to draft a full evaluation report?
options: It can accelerate structuring and first drafts but cannot replace evaluator judgement and verification
It can produce a final, submission-ready report with no human input
It can collect the field data itself
It guarantees donor approval
questions.explanation: AI speeds drafting but the evaluator must supply judgement, context, and fact-checking for a credible report.

questions.q: Adding 'If you are unsure, say so rather than guessing' to a prompt is a technique to:
options: Force citations
Make the model always refuse
Increase response length
Reduce confident hallucinations by legitimising uncertainty
questions.explanation: Explicitly permitting 'I don't know' lowers the pressure to fabricate, curbing overconfident wrong answers.

questions.q: When prompting for a Theory of Change, asking the model to make assumptions explicit is valuable because:
options: Surfaced assumptions can be tested and are central to a credible causal logic
The model cannot write assumptions
It hides weaknesses in the logic
Assumptions make the output longer
questions.explanation: A Theory of Change depends on assumptions; naming them lets the team scrutinise the causal pathway.

questions.q: Which of the following most improves a prompt asking the AI to critique a survey questionnaire?
options: Telling it to be positive
Specifying the criteria to critique against, such as leading questions, clarity, and bias
Providing no survey text
Asking simply 'is this good?'
questions.explanation: Naming explicit critique criteria focuses the model on the dimensions you care about, yielding actionable feedback.

questions.q: A limitation of relying on prompting for numeric analysis is that language models:
options: Always compute perfectly
May make arithmetic errors and should not be trusted for precise calculations without checking
Refuse all math tasks
Cannot output numbers at all
questions.explanation: LLMs can miscalculate; numeric results need verification or a dedicated calculation tool.

questions.q: The main reason to include the intended AUDIENCE in a report-drafting prompt is to:
options: Prevent hallucination entirely
Shape the tone, technical depth, and terminology to suit that reader
Increase the token count
Make the model faster
questions.explanation: Audience information lets the model calibrate language and detail, e.g. a donor board versus community members.

questions.q: Which is the best example of iterating on a prompt after a weak first result?
options: Sending the exact same prompt again
Adding a missing constraint the model ignored, such as 'each indicator must be quantitative'
Deleting all context
Switching to a longer word count only
questions.explanation: Effective iteration diagnoses what went wrong and adds the specific constraint that fixes it.

questions.q: When an AI is asked to disaggregate indicators by sex, age, and disability, providing the categories explicitly helps because:
options: The model cannot disaggregate otherwise
It makes the prompt shorter
It ensures the model uses your intended disaggregation dimensions rather than assuming others
It removes the need for data
questions.explanation: Specifying disaggregation categories aligns the output with your reporting requirements instead of the model's defaults.

questions.q: A prompt asking the model to 'draft, then critique, then revise' an indicator set is leveraging:
options: Translation between languages
Reduced temperature only
Random sampling
Self-review or reflection to catch weaknesses within a single workflow
questions.explanation: Prompting the model to critique and revise its own draft is a reflection technique that can improve quality.

questions.q: Why can pasting an entire 200-page report into a single prompt be problematic?
options: The model reads faster with more text
It may exceed the context window or dilute focus, degrading the response
Longer inputs are always more accurate
It automatically summarises without instruction
questions.explanation: Very long inputs can hit context limits or bury the relevant part, so targeted excerpts often work better.

questions.q: When prompting for evaluation questions aligned to OECD-DAC criteria, the best practice is to:
options: Ask for 'good evaluation questions'
Name the specific criteria (relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, impact, sustainability) you want covered
Let the model choose any framework
Provide no framework at all
questions.explanation: Naming the criteria ensures the questions map onto the framework your evaluation must use.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT reliably solved by better prompting alone?
options: Assigning the model a reviewer role
Getting output in a table
Ensuring the model has access to your organisation's private, current M&E database
Requesting a concise summary
questions.explanation: Access to private, current data requires supplying that data or connecting tools; prompting wording alone cannot provide it.

questions.q: Giving an AI a bad example alongside good ones (a 'negative example') can help by:
options: Doubling the cost with no benefit
Confusing the model into failing
Showing the model what to avoid, sharpening the boundary of acceptable output
Forcing a refusal
questions.explanation: Contrasting good and bad examples clarifies the decision boundary, helping the model avoid known mistakes.

questions.q: The safest way to use AI-generated indicator targets is to:
options: Treat them as suggestions to be validated against baselines and stakeholder input
Adopt them directly into the logframe
Report them to donors as evidence-based
Assume they reflect your programme's real capacity
questions.explanation: AI suggestions lack knowledge of your baselines and capacity, so targets must be validated by the team.

questions.q: A prompt that outputs a rubric-scored assessment (e.g., each criterion rated 1-5 with justification) is useful for evaluation because it:
options: Hides the reasoning behind a single number
Prevents the AI from explaining itself
Makes the AI's judgement transparent and comparable across items
Guarantees objectivity
questions.explanation: Per-criterion scores with justifications make assessments transparent and comparable, though still needing human review.

questions.q: When the model produces a plausible but unverifiable claim in a draft, the M&E practitioner should:
options: Ask the model if it is sure and accept the reply
Delete the entire draft
Assume it is correct because it sounds authoritative
Verify it against source documents before including it
questions.explanation: Plausibility is not proof; unverifiable claims must be checked against sources, and asking the model to self-confirm is unreliable.

questions.q: Which addition most helps a prompt produce a stakeholder-appropriate executive summary?
options: Provide no length guidance
State the length, reading level, and the three key messages it must convey
Ask for 'a summary'
Request maximum technical jargon
questions.explanation: Specifying length, reading level, and required messages steers the summary toward its intended purpose and reader.

questions.q: A core reason to keep a human in the loop despite good prompting is that language models:
options: Are incapable of following instructions
Cannot generate text
Always produce identical output
Lack accountability and contextual judgement for high-stakes evaluation decisions
questions.explanation: Models cannot be accountable and miss real-world context, so human judgement remains essential for consequential decisions.

questions.q: The single most important habit for effective prompt engineering in M&E is to:
options: Trust the first output completely
Review outputs critically and iteratively refine prompts based on observed errors
Use the longest prompt possible every time
Avoid giving the model any context
questions.explanation: Critical review plus iterative refinement is the durable skill that produces reliable, fit-for-purpose AI outputs.

questions.q: An M&E officer asks an AI chatbot to draft the findings section of an evaluation report. What is the single most important first step before using the output?
options: Publish it immediately to save time
Verify every factual claim and data point against the actual evaluation data
Add more AI-generated paragraphs to lengthen it
Change the font to match the donor template
questions.explanation: AI drafts can contain inaccuracies or invented details, so all claims must be checked against the real evaluation evidence before use.

questions.q: What is a 'hallucinated citation' in the context of AI-assisted report writing?
options: A correctly formatted reference to a real study
A citation deliberately omitted by the author
A footnote translated into another language
A reference the AI fabricates that looks real but does not exist
questions.explanation: AI models frequently generate plausible-looking but entirely fabricated citations, so every reference must be independently verified.

questions.q: When AI synthesises evidence across multiple studies, what is 'false synthesis'?
options: Combining studies with identical methods
Correctly weighting studies by sample size
Presenting a coherent-sounding conclusion not actually supported by the underlying studies
Excluding low-quality studies from a review
questions.explanation: False synthesis occurs when AI smooths disparate or contradictory findings into a confident narrative the evidence does not support.

questions.q: Why should evaluators be cautious about the confident tone of AI-generated summaries?
options: Confident tone always signals accuracy
AI expresses high confidence regardless of whether the underlying content is correct
Confidence indicates the model checked its sources
Tone has no effect on how readers interpret findings
questions.explanation: AI outputs are often fluent and confident even when wrong, which can mislead readers into over-trusting unverified claims.

questions.q: What does 'maintaining the evaluator's voice' mean when using AI to draft reports?
options: Using the AI's default writing style unchanged
Ensuring the final report reflects the evaluator's judgement, framing, and professional interpretation
Recording an audio version of the report
Letting the AI decide all conclusions
questions.explanation: The evaluator's independent judgement and interpretation must remain central; AI is a drafting aid, not the author of conclusions.

questions.q: A donor requires transparency about AI use in an evaluation. What is the appropriate practice?
options: Hide any AI involvement to appear more rigorous
Claim the entire report was AI-generated even if it was not
Only disclose AI use if directly asked
Disclose how and where AI tools were used in the report methodology
questions.explanation: Ethical transparency requires proactively disclosing how AI tools contributed to the evaluation process.

questions.q: Which of these is a legitimate use of AI in evidence synthesis?
options: Inventing data to fill gaps in the evidence base
Drafting a first-pass summary of documents the evaluator then verifies and refines
Fabricating citations to strengthen conclusions
Replacing the evaluator's judgement entirely
questions.explanation: AI can accelerate a first draft of a synthesis, but the evaluator must verify, correct, and own the final analysis.

questions.q: Why is 'over-confidence' a particular risk when AI generates narrative summaries of findings?
options: It makes reports too short
It always slows down the writing process
Fluent, assertive language can mask uncertainty and weak evidence
It improves the reliability of conclusions
questions.explanation: AI's assured prose can obscure genuine uncertainty in the data, leading readers to over-interpret findings.

questions.q: An AI summarises 20 project reports and states 'the programme was highly effective.' What should the evaluator do?
options: Accept it because AI processed all the reports
Trace the claim back to specific evidence and check for contradicting findings
Add exclamation marks for emphasis
Delete all the source reports to save space
questions.explanation: Any AI-generated conclusion must be traced to and validated against the underlying evidence, including disconfirming data.

questions.q: What is the best way to reduce the risk of AI fabricating references in a literature review?
options: Ask the AI to write more references
Trust the AI's memory of publications
Use a longer prompt with no source checking
Require the AI to only use sources you provide and verify each one exists
questions.explanation: Grounding the AI in supplied, verifiable sources and checking each citation minimises fabrication.

questions.q: Which statement about AI-generated data visualisations for M&E reports is most accurate?
options: AI charts never misrepresent data
AI may mislabel axes, invent values, or distort scales, so charts must be checked against source data
Visuals from AI require no verification
AI always chooses the most honest chart type
questions.explanation: AI-produced visuals can contain errors or distortions, so they must be validated against the actual dataset.

questions.q: Why should an evaluator avoid pasting confidential beneficiary data into a public AI chatbot?
options: It slows down the model
It can breach data protection and confidentiality commitments
Public chatbots produce better summaries with private data
There is no risk if the data is small
questions.explanation: Sharing sensitive or personal data with third-party AI services can violate privacy, consent, and data-protection obligations.

questions.q: What is 'triangulation' and how does it relate to fact-checking AI output?
options: Using three AI models to write faster
Formatting reports in three columns
Cross-checking a claim against multiple independent sources or methods
Asking the AI the same question three times
questions.explanation: Triangulation verifies findings across independent sources, an essential check on AI-generated claims.

questions.q: An AI tool produces a polished executive summary but omits a key negative finding present in the data. This illustrates which risk?
options: Improved objectivity
Selective or incomplete synthesis that can mislead decision-makers
Better data protection
Enhanced transparency
questions.explanation: AI may under-represent inconvenient findings, so evaluators must ensure the summary reflects the full evidence.

questions.q: When is disclosing AI use in an evaluation report especially important?
options: Only when the report is short
When AI materially shaped analysis, synthesis, or conclusions
Never, as it undermines credibility
Only for internal drafts
questions.explanation: Material AI contributions to analysis or conclusions should be disclosed for accountability and credibility.

questions.q: Which practice best preserves evaluator judgement while using AI for drafting?
options: Accepting AI conclusions without review
Letting AI select which stakeholders to interview
Removing the evaluator from the analysis stage
Using AI for structure and language while the evaluator determines and validates all findings
questions.explanation: AI can assist with drafting mechanics, but the evaluator must retain control over findings and interpretation.

questions.q: What is a key limitation of AI when synthesising qualitative interview data?
options: It perfectly captures all context and nuance
It may miss context, misattribute quotes, or flatten nuanced perspectives
It cannot process any text
It always cites the correct respondent
questions.explanation: AI can lose contextual nuance and misattribute or fabricate quotes, requiring careful human verification.

questions.q: An evaluator uses AI to translate a report into a local South Asian language. What quality check is essential?
options: No check is needed for AI translation
A fluent human reviewer should verify accuracy and cultural appropriateness
Only checking the word count
Assuming the translation is perfect if it looks fluent
questions.explanation: AI translations can contain subtle errors or cultural mismatches that a fluent human reviewer must catch.

questions.q: Why is it risky to let AI generate the 'recommendations' section of an evaluation autonomously?
options: Recommendations must reflect contextual judgement and stakeholder realities the AI cannot fully grasp
AI recommendations are always context-specific
It is the fastest and safest section for AI
Recommendations require no human input
questions.explanation: Recommendations depend on deep contextual and political understanding that requires evaluator judgement, not just AI drafting.

questions.q: What does 'grounding' an AI mean in evidence synthesis?
options: Turning off the AI
Providing the AI with specific source documents to base its output on
Letting the AI use only its training data
Asking the AI to be more creative
questions.explanation: Grounding constrains the AI to supplied sources, reducing fabrication and improving traceability.

questions.q: An AI-generated meta-summary combines findings from studies with conflicting results into one positive conclusion. What is the correct evaluator response?
options: Publish the positive conclusion
Surface and report the conflict rather than let AI paper over it
Delete the conflicting studies
Ask AI to make the conclusion even stronger
questions.explanation: Conflicting evidence should be transparently reported, not smoothed away by an AI-generated synthesis.

questions.q: Which is the most reliable way to fact-check a statistic an AI included in a draft report?
options: Ask the AI if it is sure
Check the figure directly in the primary dataset or source document
Assume it is right if it sounds plausible
Compare it to a different AI's guess
questions.explanation: Statistics must be verified against the primary data source, not the AI's self-assessment.

questions.q: What is a responsible way to describe AI use in an evaluation's methodology section?
options: Omit it entirely
State which tools were used, for what tasks, and how outputs were verified
Say only that 'technology was used'
Claim AI did all analysis when it did not
questions.explanation: Clear, specific disclosure of tools, tasks, and verification steps supports transparency and reproducibility.

questions.q: Why can AI-assisted evidence synthesis introduce bias?
options: It removes all human bias automatically
It can reflect biases in its training data or in how documents are selected and prompted
It weights all evidence perfectly
Bias is impossible in automated systems
questions.explanation: AI inherits biases from training data and from human choices about inputs and prompts, so outputs need scrutiny.

questions.q: An evaluator notices the AI draft attributes a finding to 'World Bank 2019' but cannot locate the report. What is the correct action?
options: Keep the citation since it sounds authoritative
Remove or replace it unless the source is verified to exist and support the claim
Add more unverified citations for balance
Change the year to 2020 and move on
questions.explanation: Unverifiable citations must be removed or replaced, as they are likely fabricated.

questions.q: How should AI be positioned within a rigorous evaluation workflow?
options: As the final decision-maker on all findings
As an assistive tool whose outputs are always reviewed by a qualified evaluator
As a replacement for the evaluation team
As a source of new primary data it invents
questions.explanation: AI should assist, not replace, the human evaluator who remains responsible for verified findings.

questions.q: What risk does 'automation bias' pose when reviewing AI-generated reports?
options: Reviewers scrutinise AI output too harshly
Reviewers over-trust AI output and skip necessary verification
AI refuses to produce output
Reports become too critical of AI
questions.explanation: Automation bias leads people to accept machine outputs uncritically, undermining verification.

questions.q: Which of the following most improves the traceability of an AI-assisted synthesis?
options: Removing all source references
Requiring the AI to link each claim to a specific source passage the evaluator can check
Using vague summaries without attribution
Letting the AI cite from memory
questions.explanation: Claim-to-source linking lets evaluators verify each statement, improving accountability.

questions.q: Why should an evaluator read the original source documents even when AI has summarised them?
options: To waste time deliberately
To confirm the summary is accurate and captures important nuances and caveats
Because AI summaries are illegal
To make the report longer
questions.explanation: Reading originals ensures the AI summary is faithful and does not omit critical context or caveats.

questions.q: What is an appropriate transparency statement for a report where AI drafted initial text?
options: 'No tools were used in this evaluation'
'AI was used to draft initial summaries, which the evaluation team reviewed, verified, and revised'
'This report is entirely machine-generated and unverified'
Say nothing about the process
questions.explanation: An honest statement notes AI's drafting role and the human verification that followed.

questions.q: An AI confidently states a programme 'reduced poverty by 40%' but the data show no measurement of poverty. This is an example of:
options: Accurate reporting
A fabricated or unsupported finding
Proper triangulation
Transparent disclosure
questions.explanation: The claim is invented because the data never measured the outcome, illustrating AI fabrication risk.

questions.q: Which approach best balances AI efficiency with evaluation integrity?
options: Use AI for everything without review
Use AI to accelerate drafting and organisation while humans verify all facts and own conclusions
Never use AI under any circumstances
Let AI publish reports directly to donors
questions.explanation: AI improves efficiency, but human verification and ownership of conclusions protect integrity.

questions.q: Why is it problematic to ask AI to 'make the findings sound more positive'?
options: It improves objectivity
It can distort evidence and misrepresent results to stakeholders
It is the standard practice in evaluation
It has no ethical implications
questions.explanation: Skewing tone to favour positive results misrepresents the evidence and violates evaluation ethics.

questions.q: When AI drafts a narrative summary, what should the evaluator check about the causal claims?
options: Nothing, causal claims from AI are reliable
Whether the evidence actually supports causation rather than mere correlation
Only the spelling
Whether the claims sound impressive
questions.explanation: AI may assert causation the data cannot support, so causal claims need careful evidentiary scrutiny.

questions.q: What is a key advantage of using AI to produce a first draft of a large document summary?
options: It guarantees accuracy
It can save time on structuring and initial drafting that the evaluator then verifies
It removes the need for any human review
It eliminates the need for source documents
questions.explanation: AI speeds up initial structuring and drafting, but the output still requires human verification.

questions.q: A team publishes an AI-written report without disclosing AI use or checking it. Which principles are violated?
options: None, this is best practice
Transparency and accuracy/verification
Only formatting standards
Only translation quality
questions.explanation: Undisclosed, unverified AI use breaches both transparency and the duty to ensure accuracy.

questions.q: How can prompts be designed to reduce AI over-confidence in synthesis?
options: Ask the AI to always sound certain
Instruct the AI to flag uncertainty, note evidence gaps, and avoid unsupported claims
Tell the AI to omit all caveats
Request only positive conclusions
questions.explanation: Prompts that request uncertainty flags and evidence limits help counter AI's tendency to over-assert.

questions.q: Why is human judgement still essential when AI ranks evidence by 'quality'?
options: AI perfectly assesses methodological rigour
AI may misjudge study rigour, relevance, or context that an expert can evaluate
Evidence quality does not matter
AI ranking is always transparent
questions.explanation: Assessing evidence quality requires methodological expertise and contextual judgement AI cannot fully replicate.

questions.q: What should an evaluator do if two AI tools give conflicting summaries of the same data?
options: Pick the more positive one
Return to the primary data to determine which, if either, is correct
Average the two summaries blindly
Assume both are equally valid
questions.explanation: Conflicting AI outputs signal the need to verify against the primary evidence directly.

questions.q: Which is a sign that an AI-generated report section needs deeper fact-checking?
options: It cites specific numbers and named studies
Precise-sounding statistics or citations that are not in your source materials
It uses simple language
It is well organised
questions.explanation: Specific figures or references absent from your sources are red flags for fabrication.

questions.q: Why should the evaluator, not the AI, decide the report's key messages?
options: The AI cannot format text
Key messages require professional judgement, contextual understanding, and accountability the evaluator holds
AI messages are always too long
It is a legal formatting requirement
questions.explanation: Key messages carry professional accountability and demand contextual judgement that belongs to the evaluator.

questions.q: What is a good practice when using AI to generate a visual summary (e.g., an infographic) of findings?
options: Trust all numbers the AI places on it
Verify every figure and label against the validated dataset before publishing
Skip verification if it looks professional
Let the AI invent illustrative statistics
questions.explanation: All figures and labels in AI visuals must be checked against validated data to avoid misrepresentation.

questions.q: How does over-reliance on AI summaries threaten the depth of an evaluation?
options: It deepens analysis automatically
Evaluators may lose direct familiarity with the evidence and miss subtle but important insights
It has no effect on analytical depth
It guarantees comprehensive coverage
questions.explanation: Depending on summaries can distance evaluators from the raw evidence, causing them to miss nuance.

questions.q: An AI drafts findings that contradict the evaluator's field observations. What is the most rigorous response?
options: Defer to the AI since it processed more text
Investigate the discrepancy against the primary evidence and the evaluator's data
Delete the field observations
Publish both without reconciling them
questions.explanation: Discrepancies should be investigated against primary evidence, not resolved by deferring to the AI.

questions.q: Which statement about AI and confidentiality in M&E is correct?
options: Any AI tool is safe for sensitive data
Data-handling and consent terms of the AI tool must be checked before uploading sensitive information
Confidentiality does not apply to digital data
AI automatically anonymises all inputs
questions.explanation: Evaluators must confirm an AI tool's data-handling terms and obtain proper consent before sharing sensitive data.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of keeping a record of prompts and AI outputs used in a report?
options: To increase file size
To support transparency, auditability, and reproducibility of the process
To hide the AI's role
To replace the source data
questions.explanation: Logging prompts and outputs makes the AI-assisted process transparent, auditable, and reproducible.

questions.q: Why might an AI-generated synthesis over-generalise from a few strong examples?
options: It weights all evidence proportionally
It can latch onto vivid or frequent patterns and present them as broadly representative
It never generalises
It only reports minority views
questions.explanation: AI may over-generalise from salient examples, so evaluators must check representativeness.

questions.q: When AI is used to draft a report, who remains professionally accountable for its accuracy?
options: The AI vendor
The evaluator and evaluation team who sign off on the report
No one, since AI wrote it
The software developers
questions.explanation: Professional accountability for the report's accuracy rests with the human evaluators who approve it.

questions.q: Which is the best overall principle for AI-assisted reporting and evidence synthesis in M&E?
options: Automate first, verify never
Use AI to assist, verify everything against evidence, disclose its use, and keep the evaluator's judgement central
Hide AI use and skip fact-checking to save time
Let AI make all conclusions and recommendations
questions.explanation: Responsible practice combines AI assistance with rigorous verification, transparency, and retained human judgement.

sections.title: Bias, Fairness & Validity in AI for M&E

questions.q: A machine learning model used to predict which villages need nutrition support is trained mostly on data from well-surveyed districts. What type of bias is most directly introduced?
options: Sampling (representation) bias
Confirmation bias
Publication bias
Anchoring bias
questions.explanation: When training data over-represents some populations and under-represents others, the model learns patterns that generalize poorly to the missing groups, a classic sampling or representation bias.

questions.q: An AI system scores loan applications and systematically disadvantages a caste group even though caste is not an input variable. This is best described as:
options: Random error
Proxy discrimination
Selection on the outcome
Measurement reliability failure
questions.explanation: Proxy discrimination occurs when a model uses correlated features (like postal code or occupation) that stand in for a protected attribute, producing discriminatory effects without using the attribute directly.

questions.q: 'Disparate impact' in an AI screening tool refers to:
options: A deliberate rule that excludes a protected group
The variance of predictions across random seeds
A neutral-seeming process that produces unequal outcomes across groups
The gap between training and test accuracy
questions.explanation: Disparate impact describes facially neutral practices or algorithms that nonetheless produce substantially unequal outcomes for a protected group, regardless of intent.

questions.q: Historical bias in training data means that:
options: The data was collected too long ago to be valid
The model gives more weight to older records
Timestamps in the dataset are incorrect
The data faithfully reflects real-world inequities that we may not want to reproduce
questions.explanation: Historical bias arises when data accurately captures existing societal inequities, so a model trained on it can perpetuate those inequities even if the data is technically correct.

questions.q: Which fairness notion requires that a model's predictions be equally accurate (e.g., equal true positive rates) across groups?
options: Equalized odds
Demographic parity
Individual fairness
Calibration by group
questions.explanation: Equalized odds requires that true positive and false positive rates be equal across groups, focusing on equal error rates rather than equal selection rates.

questions.q: Demographic parity (statistical parity) is satisfied when:
options: The model has the same accuracy for all groups
The proportion receiving a positive prediction is equal across groups
Every individual is treated identically
The false negative rate is zero
questions.explanation: Demographic parity requires that the rate of positive outcomes be equal across groups, independent of the true underlying base rates.

questions.q: An M&E team finds their AI classifier flags 'high-risk dropout' students, but the label was based on teachers' past referrals, which were biased against girls. This is an example of:
options: Overfitting
Data leakage from the test set
Label bias in the target variable
Hyperparameter mis-tuning
questions.explanation: When the outcome label itself encodes human bias, the model learns to reproduce that bias; this is label or target bias, distinct from feature bias.

questions.q: Why can AI systems amplify existing inequities rather than merely reflect them?
options: They always use random sampling
They are audited too frequently
They cannot process categorical variables
Feedback loops can reinforce biased predictions as they shape future data
questions.explanation: When biased predictions drive decisions that generate new data (e.g., over-policing an area produces more recorded crime there), feedback loops entrench and amplify the original bias.

questions.q: A key limitation of removing a protected attribute (like gender) from model inputs to achieve fairness is that:
options: Correlated proxy features can still encode the attribute
It always reduces model accuracy to zero
It violates data protection law
It makes the model non-deterministic
questions.explanation: 'Fairness through unawareness' fails because other features correlated with the protected attribute act as proxies, so the model can still discriminate.

questions.q: In M&E, 'measurement validity' when AI is in the pipeline is threatened when:
options: The dataset is stored in the cloud
The AI proxy indicator diverges from the real construct it is meant to measure
The model runs slowly
The team uses open-source tools
questions.explanation: Validity concerns whether the AI-derived measure actually captures the intended construct; if an AI proxy drifts from what it claims to measure, conclusions about program impact become invalid.

questions.q: Satellite imagery is used by an AI model to estimate poverty, but cloud cover is more common in certain regions, degrading predictions there. This is primarily a threat to:
options: Model interpretability
Data encryption
Representativeness and equal measurement quality across regions
User consent
questions.explanation: Systematically poorer data quality in some regions produces uneven measurement accuracy, undermining representativeness and fair comparison across areas.

questions.q: Which of the following is a data-level (pre-processing) bias mitigation strategy?
options: Adjusting the decision threshold after training
Adding a fairness constraint to the loss function
Post-hoc calibration of scores
Re-weighting or re-sampling the training data to balance groups
questions.explanation: Pre-processing methods modify the training data itself, for example by re-weighting or re-sampling to reduce representation imbalance before the model is trained.

questions.q: An 'in-processing' fairness intervention works by:
options: Incorporating fairness constraints or penalties into the model's training objective
Cleaning the raw data before training
Changing predictions only after the model is deployed
Deleting the model entirely
questions.explanation: In-processing methods embed fairness directly into the learning algorithm, such as adding a regularization term that penalizes disparities during training.

questions.q: A 'post-processing' bias mitigation approach typically involves:
options: Rebalancing the dataset
Adjusting decision thresholds separately per group to equalize error rates
Retraining with a fairness penalty
Collecting entirely new data
questions.explanation: Post-processing adjusts model outputs after training, for example by setting group-specific thresholds to equalize false positive or negative rates.

questions.q: The 'impossibility of fairness' result shows that:
options: No AI model can ever be accurate
Fairness is illegal in most countries
Several common fairness metrics cannot all be satisfied simultaneously when base rates differ
Bias can always be fully removed with enough data
questions.explanation: When base rates differ across groups, calibration, equalized odds, and demographic parity generally cannot all hold at once, forcing explicit trade-offs.

questions.q: An enumerator collects survey data only from households present during daytime visits, missing those who migrate for work. The resulting AI model suffers from:
options: Simpson's paradox
Multicollinearity
Regression to the mean
Selection bias
questions.explanation: Systematically excluding a subgroup during data collection produces selection bias, so the sample is not representative of the target population.

questions.q: Why is a held-out test set drawn from the same biased source as the training set inadequate for detecting bias?
options: It shares the same biases, so it can validate a biased model as 'accurate'
It is too small
It cannot compute accuracy
Test sets are never labeled
questions.explanation: If the test set inherits the same biases as training data, standard accuracy metrics look good while the model still performs poorly on under-represented real-world groups.

questions.q: Disaggregated evaluation in M&E means:
options: Splitting the model into smaller models
Reporting model performance separately for relevant subgroups (gender, region, caste)
Removing outliers before scoring
Averaging metrics across all data
questions.explanation: Disaggregating performance by subgroup reveals disparities that aggregate metrics hide, which is essential for detecting unfair outcomes.

questions.q: A model is 'well-calibrated by group' when:
options: It has equal accuracy for everyone
It never makes errors
Among those given a predicted probability of X%, about X% actually experience the outcome, within each group
It uses the same threshold for all
questions.explanation: Group calibration means predicted probabilities match observed frequencies within each group, so a 70% risk score means the same thing across groups.

questions.q: Which scenario best illustrates 'aggregation bias'?
options: Data is stored in aggregate tables
Survey responses are summed incorrectly
The model uses too many features
A single model is applied to groups for whom the relationship between features and outcome genuinely differs
questions.explanation: Aggregation bias occurs when one model is forced onto distinct subpopulations that have different underlying relationships, so it fits none of them well.

questions.q: An AI tool translating open-ended survey responses performs worse for a regional dialect. In M&E terms this most threatens:
options: Construct validity of the coded responses for that group
Data storage costs
Sampling frame completeness
Randomization integrity
questions.explanation: Poor translation distorts the meaning captured for that group, undermining construct validity and creating unequal measurement quality.

questions.q: 'Representativeness' of training data refers to:
options: How visually appealing the dataset is
How well the sample reflects the population the model will serve
The number of columns in the data
Whether data is encrypted
questions.explanation: Representativeness measures whether the training sample's composition matches the real target population, which is fundamental to generalizable, fair predictions.

questions.q: A facial-analysis attendance system has higher error rates for darker-skinned women. The root cause is most likely:
options: Excessive regularization
Too high a learning rate
Under-representation of that group in training data
Using a validation set
questions.explanation: Well-documented facial analysis disparities stem largely from training datasets that under-represent darker-skinned and female faces, degrading accuracy for that intersection.

questions.q: 'Intersectional' bias analysis is important because:
options: It only matters for image data
It reduces the need for disaggregation
It always improves accuracy
Disparities can appear at combinations of attributes (e.g., rural women) even when each single attribute looks fair
questions.explanation: A model can appear fair on gender and on region separately yet fail badly for their intersection, so intersectional analysis is needed to catch hidden harms.

questions.q: When an AI model's predictions are used to allocate scarce program resources, a false negative for a needy household means:
options: An eligible beneficiary is wrongly excluded from support
Nothing, since predictions are advisory
The model runs faster
Data privacy is improved
questions.explanation: A false negative means a genuinely eligible or at-risk person is not flagged, causing exclusion errors that can concentrate on already-marginalized groups.

questions.q: 'Exclusion error' concentrated in a marginalized group is a fairness concern because:
options: It only affects model speed
It compounds existing disadvantage by denying support to those most in need
It improves calibration
It is required by demographic parity
questions.explanation: When those wrongly denied benefits are disproportionately from disadvantaged groups, the AI deepens rather than reduces inequity.

questions.q: A robust way to test an AI model for bias before deployment is to:
options: Check overall accuracy only
Confirm the code compiles
Run a disaggregated audit comparing error rates across protected groups
Ask the developers if it is fair
questions.explanation: A fairness audit computes and compares performance metrics across subgroups, surfacing disparities that a single aggregate accuracy figure conceals.

questions.q: 'Concept drift' can undermine validity of an AI M&E indicator when:
options: The dataset is duplicated
The model uses fewer features
The team changes vendors
The relationship between inputs and the target changes over time after deployment
questions.explanation: Concept drift occurs when real-world relationships shift over time, so a once-valid model becomes inaccurate and its indicators lose validity unless monitored and retrained.

questions.q: Which is the strongest reason to involve affected communities in reviewing an AI M&E tool?
options: They can identify context-specific harms and invalid proxies that developers miss
It speeds up model training
It removes the need for testing
It guarantees demographic parity
questions.explanation: Local stakeholders understand context and can flag proxies, harms, and validity problems that are invisible to external developers, improving both fairness and validity.

questions.q: An AI chatbot collecting beneficiary feedback is only accessible via smartphone. The resulting data suffers from:
options: Overfitting
Coverage/access bias excluding those without smartphones
Label noise
Gradient explosion
questions.explanation: Restricting the channel excludes people without the required technology, producing coverage bias so the feedback is unrepresentative of the full population.

questions.q: The main risk of using AI-predicted values as if they were ground-truth measurements in impact evaluation is:
options: Predictions are always exactly correct
It reduces sample size
Prediction error can be correlated with treatment or group, biasing impact estimates
It requires more enumerators
questions.explanation: If AI measurement error is systematically related to treatment status or subgroup, plugging predictions in as truth can bias impact estimates in unpredictable directions.

questions.q: 'Automation bias' among M&E staff refers to:
options: The model automating data entry
Bias caused by faster computers
The automatic deletion of data
The tendency to over-trust AI outputs and under-scrutinize errors
questions.explanation: Automation bias is the human tendency to accept algorithmic recommendations uncritically, which can let biased or invalid AI outputs go unchallenged.

questions.q: Which practice best supports transparency about an AI model's bias limitations?
options: Publishing a model/data documentation card describing data sources, intended use, and known disparities
Hiding the training data details
Encrypting the model weights
Increasing the number of parameters
questions.explanation: Documentation artifacts like model cards and datasheets disclose data provenance, intended use, and known performance gaps, enabling informed and fair deployment.

questions.q: A predictive model for school dropout is trained on data where dropouts were only recorded when a teacher noticed. This is an example of:
options: Perfect labeling
Measurement bias in the outcome
Class balance
Cross-validation
questions.explanation: When the outcome is only observed through an imperfect, biased recording process, the recorded label systematically misrepresents the true outcome, a measurement bias.

questions.q: Why does high overall accuracy NOT guarantee fairness?
options: Accuracy is always low
Accuracy measures fairness directly
A model can be accurate for the majority while failing a small but important minority
Fairness requires 100% accuracy
questions.explanation: Aggregate accuracy is dominated by the majority group, so a model can post high accuracy while performing poorly for a minority, masking serious disparities.

questions.q: 'Simpson's paradox' is relevant to AM&E bias analysis because:
options: It proves models are always fair
It only applies to images
It measures encryption strength
A trend visible in aggregate data can reverse when data is disaggregated by group
questions.explanation: Simpson's paradox shows aggregate relationships can reverse within subgroups, underscoring why disaggregated analysis is essential for valid and fair conclusions.

questions.q: Which action reduces sampling bias when building a training dataset for a rural livelihoods model?
options: Deliberately oversampling under-represented regions and groups
Using only the easiest-to-reach villages
Dropping all minority-group records
Ignoring geographic spread
questions.explanation: Purposive oversampling of under-represented segments improves representativeness so the model learns adequate patterns for those groups.

questions.q: A fairness metric that focuses on treating similar individuals similarly, regardless of group, is called:
options: Demographic parity
Individual fairness
Equal opportunity
Predictive parity
questions.explanation: Individual fairness holds that individuals who are similar with respect to the task should receive similar predictions, a person-level rather than group-level criterion.

questions.q: 'Equal opportunity' as a fairness criterion specifically requires equal:
options: Positive prediction rates across groups
Numbers of features per group
True positive rates across groups
Training times across groups
questions.explanation: Equal opportunity requires equal true positive rates across groups, meaning qualified individuals have the same chance of a positive prediction regardless of group.

questions.q: An NGO uses a globally trained AI model without local validation in South Asia. The main validity risk is:
options: Faster inference
Reduced storage needs
Improved calibration
Distribution shift making the model invalid for the local context
questions.explanation: Distribution shift between the training context and the local deployment context can make the model's predictions systematically invalid unless re-validated locally.

questions.q: Which is a symptom that a proxy indicator produced by AI lacks validity?
options: It diverges from ground-truth measurements differently across subgroups
It correlates strongly with the true construct in all groups
It is easy to compute
It has a clear name
questions.explanation: If an AI proxy tracks the true construct well for some groups but poorly for others, it lacks measurement validity and will produce misleading, inequitable conclusions.

questions.q: The safest way to interpret an AI risk score used for targeting is to treat it as:
options: An infallible measure of need
One imperfect input to be combined with human judgment and other evidence
A legal determination
A random number
questions.explanation: AI scores carry bias and error, so treating them as one input alongside human review and other data guards against over-reliance and unfair automated exclusion.

questions.q: 'Predictive parity' (calibration-based fairness) is violated when:
options: The model runs on different hardware
Groups have equal sample sizes
The same score implies different actual outcome rates for different groups
Features are standardized
questions.explanation: Predictive parity requires that a given predicted score correspond to the same real outcome probability across groups; unequal calibration violates it.

questions.q: A reason AI can entrench inequity in resource-poor settings is:
options: Models refuse to run without full data
Poor regions have too much data
AI ignores all geographic data
Data is most abundant for already-advantaged, well-connected populations
questions.explanation: Data availability skews toward advantaged, digitally connected populations, so models are trained to serve them best and under-serve the marginalized.

questions.q: To test whether a model discriminates via proxies, an analyst can:
options: Check whether protected-group membership is predictable from the model's inputs
Delete the outcome variable
Increase the learning rate
Reduce the test set to zero
questions.explanation: If a protected attribute can be accurately predicted from the remaining features, those features can serve as proxies, signaling risk of proxy discrimination.

questions.q: Which best describes 'evaluation bias' in AI?
options: Bias introduced by program evaluators
Using a benchmark or metric that does not represent the deployment population
The cost of running evaluations
Bias in academic peer review
questions.explanation: Evaluation bias arises when the test benchmark or metric is unrepresentative of the real deployment population, so reported performance overstates real-world fairness and accuracy.

questions.q: A defensible fairness goal-setting step before deploying an AI M&E tool is to:
options: Assume all fairness metrics can be maximized together
Avoid documenting any decisions
Explicitly decide which fairness definition matters for the context and the acceptable trade-offs
Let the model choose its own objective
questions.explanation: Because fairness definitions conflict, teams must deliberately choose which criterion aligns with their values and context and accept the resulting trade-offs transparently.

questions.q: Large language models used to code qualitative M&E data may introduce bias because:
options: They cannot process text
They always output numbers
They require no prompts
They reflect biases in their vast, uncurated training corpora
questions.explanation: LLMs absorb societal and cultural biases from their training data, which can surface as skewed or stereotyped coding of qualitative responses.

questions.q: Continuous post-deployment monitoring for bias is necessary primarily because:
options: Models and populations change over time, so fairness at launch does not guarantee fairness later
It reduces electricity use
It is required to compile the code
It removes the need for initial testing
questions.explanation: Data drift, concept drift, and feedback loops mean a model that was fair at deployment can become biased over time, requiring ongoing monitoring.

questions.q: Which statement about the relationship between bias, fairness, and validity is most accurate?
options: They are unrelated concerns
Biased or unrepresentative data can undermine both fairness across groups and the overall validity of AI-derived measures
Validity only concerns speed
Fairness guarantees validity automatically
questions.explanation: Bias in data and design threatens fairness (equitable treatment across groups) and validity (whether the measure means what it claims), so the two concerns are deeply intertwined.

questions.q: In the context of using AI tools to analyze survey data collected from beneficiaries, what does 'informed consent for AI use' primarily require?
options: That respondents are asked to create accounts on the AI platform
That respondents are told their data may be processed by AI systems and understand the implications before agreeing
That the M&E team obtains a signed liability waiver from the AI vendor
That consent is only needed if the AI produces a published report
questions.explanation: Informed consent for AI use means participants are clearly told that AI may process their data and understand what that entails before they agree.

questions.q: India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act was enacted in which year?
questions.explanation: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act was passed in 2023, establishing the country's first comprehensive personal data protection framework.

questions.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023, the individual whose personal data is being processed is referred to as the:
options: Data Fiduciary
Data Processor
Consent Manager
Data Principal
questions.explanation: The DPDP Act 2023 uses the term 'Data Principal' for the individual to whom the personal data relates.

questions.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023, an entity that determines the purpose and means of processing personal data is called the:
options: Data Principal
Data Consumer
Data Auditor
Data Fiduciary
questions.explanation: The DPDP Act 2023 defines the 'Data Fiduciary' as the person or entity that determines the purpose and means of processing personal data.

questions.q: A common privacy risk when pasting raw beneficiary interview transcripts into a public consumer AI chatbot is that:
options: Sensitive personal data may be stored or used to train third-party models without consent
The transcript will be encrypted end-to-end by default
The AI will automatically anonymize all names
The data becomes legally exempt from privacy law once processed by AI
questions.explanation: Consumer AI services may retain inputs and use them for model training, exposing sensitive personal data shared without the data principal's consent.

questions.q: 'De-identification' of a dataset before AI processing primarily involves:
options: Encrypting the file with a password
Removing or masking direct and indirect identifiers so individuals cannot be readily recognized
Deleting the entire dataset after analysis
Translating the data into a local language
questions.explanation: De-identification removes or masks identifiers so that individuals cannot be readily re-identified from the data.

questions.q: Which of the following is a DIRECT identifier that should typically be removed during de-identification?
options: The year of a program's launch
The total number of survey respondents
A respondent's full name and phone number
The district-level average income
questions.explanation: A full name and phone number directly identify an individual and are classic direct identifiers to remove.

questions.q: Why can removing only names still leave a dataset re-identifiable?
options: Because de-identification always requires deleting the data
Because combinations of quasi-identifiers like age, village, and occupation can single out individuals
Because AI cannot read anonymized data
Because names are the only identifiers that matter legally
questions.explanation: Quasi-identifiers such as age, small-area location, and occupation can combine to uniquely single out a person even without names.

questions.q: The 'do-no-harm' principle in AI-assisted M&E most directly requires evaluators to:
options: Publish all raw data openly for transparency
Ensure that AI use does not expose participants or communities to new risks or harms
Avoid documenting any limitations of the analysis
Maximize the number of AI tools used per evaluation
questions.explanation: Do-no-harm requires that the use of AI does not create new risks or harms for participants or communities.

questions.q: Transparency about AI use in an evaluation report is best demonstrated by:
options: Disclosing where and how AI tools were used and their limitations
Claiming all analysis was done manually to appear more rigorous
Listing the AI vendor's stock price
Hiding AI use to avoid confusing stakeholders
questions.explanation: Transparency means openly disclosing where and how AI tools were used, along with their limitations.

questions.q: A 'dual-use risk' in the context of AI for M&E refers to:
options: Using two different AI models for the same task
Sharing costs of AI subscriptions between two projects
Running an evaluation in two languages
The possibility that a tool or data built for beneficial purposes could be repurposed to cause harm
questions.explanation: Dual-use risk is the danger that technology or data created for good could be repurposed to harm people.

questions.q: Which practice best supports accountability when AI contributes to evaluation findings?
options: Preventing anyone from questioning the AI output
Maintaining human oversight and keeping a clear record of AI's role and decisions
Deleting the analysis logs after the report is submitted
Attributing all conclusions solely to the AI system
questions.explanation: Accountability requires human oversight and a clear, auditable record of how AI was used in reaching conclusions.

questions.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023, consent obtained from a Data Principal must generally be:
options: Free, informed, specific, and unambiguous with a clear affirmative action
Valid only if given verbally
Implied automatically once the survey begins
Bundled into a single blanket approval for all future uses
questions.explanation: The DPDP Act requires consent to be free, informed, specific, unambiguous, and given through a clear affirmative action.

questions.q: When an M&E team wants to send children's data to an AI service, the DPDP Act 2023 generally requires:
options: No additional safeguards beyond adult data
Only the child's own consent
A one-time fee to the regulator
Verifiable consent of a parent or lawful guardian and restrictions on harmful processing
questions.explanation: The DPDP Act mandates verifiable parental or guardian consent and prohibits processing that is detrimental to a child's wellbeing.

questions.q: Which is the safest approach before using a third-party cloud AI service on sensitive M&E data?
options: Upload everything to test the tool's capabilities
Assume the vendor complies with all laws without checking
Rely on the AI to flag any privacy problems itself
Review the vendor's data retention, security, and training-use policies and de-identify data first
questions.explanation: Due diligence on vendor policies plus de-identifying data before upload minimizes privacy exposure to third parties.

questions.q: A core principle of 'responsible AI' that addresses unequal outcomes across social groups is:
options: Profitability
Speed
Fairness and non-discrimination
Model size
questions.explanation: Fairness and non-discrimination aim to prevent AI systems from producing unequal or discriminatory outcomes across groups.

questions.q: 'Purpose limitation' as a data-protection principle means:
options: Data must be limited to one page per respondent
Data can be used for any future purpose the organization invents
Data should only be used for the specific purposes for which it was collected and consented to
Only senior staff may define the purpose
questions.explanation: Purpose limitation restricts data use to the specific, consented purposes for which it was originally collected.

questions.q: 'Data minimization' in AI-assisted evaluation advises practitioners to:
options: Collect and share only the personal data actually needed for the task
Reduce the length of the final report
Minimize the number of evaluators
Collect as much data as possible in case it is useful later
questions.explanation: Data minimization means collecting and processing only the personal data strictly necessary for the intended purpose.

questions.q: If an AI summarization tool fabricates a quote that no respondent actually said, this is an example of:
options: Acceptable creative interpretation
Proper de-identification
A privacy breach only
A hallucination that threatens the accuracy and integrity of findings
questions.explanation: AI 'hallucinations' fabricate content that was never in the source data, undermining the accuracy and credibility of evaluation findings.

questions.q: Which statement about AI bias in M&E is most accurate?
options: AI can reproduce or amplify biases present in its training data, affecting marginalized groups
Bias only occurs when AI is used in finance
AI models are neutral and cannot reflect bias
Bias disappears once data is anonymized
questions.explanation: AI systems learn from data and can reproduce or amplify existing biases, disproportionately affecting marginalized groups.

questions.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023, the regulatory body established to oversee compliance is the:
options: Reserve Bank of India
Central Statistics Office
National Human Rights Commission
Data Protection Board of India
questions.explanation: The DPDP Act 2023 establishes the Data Protection Board of India to adjudicate and enforce compliance.

questions.q: A key reason to keep a 'human-in-the-loop' when AI codes qualitative data is to:
options: Prevent the AI from ever being used again
Eliminate the need for any documentation
Catch errors, context misinterpretations, and biased outputs before they inform decisions
Slow down the process for billing purposes
questions.explanation: Human oversight catches AI errors, misread context, and bias before flawed outputs shape important decisions.

questions.q: Which of these best describes 'sensitive personal data' that warrants extra protection in M&E?
options: The date the evaluation was commissioned
Health status, caste, religion, sexual orientation, or disability of respondents
The project's budget line items
The name of the funding agency
questions.explanation: Data on health, caste, religion, sexuality, or disability is sensitive because its misuse can lead to serious harm or discrimination.

questions.q: Before feeding GPS coordinates of vulnerable households into an AI mapping tool, the primary concern is:
options: Precise locations could expose at-risk individuals to targeting or harm
The tool may render maps too slowly
AI cannot process numeric data
Coordinates are never considered personal data
questions.explanation: Precise geolocation of vulnerable people is highly sensitive because it can enable targeting, surveillance, or physical harm.

questions.q: Disclosing AI use to respondents during consent is important because it:
