options: Transfers all legal liability to the respondents
Respects their autonomy and right to know how their data will be processed
Is only a marketing requirement
Guarantees the AI will not make mistakes
questions.explanation: Disclosure respects respondents' autonomy and their right to understand how their personal data will be handled.

questions.q: Which is an appropriate governance measure for AI use in an evaluation organization?
options: Letting each staff member use any AI tool without guidance
Banning all documentation of AI decisions
An internal AI-use policy defining approved tools, data handling rules, and oversight
Outsourcing all ethical judgments to the AI vendor
questions.explanation: A clear internal AI-use policy defining approved tools, data rules, and oversight is a foundational governance measure.

questions.q: The principle of 'explainability' in responsible AI means that:
options: It should be possible to understand and communicate how the AI reached its outputs
Explanations must always be in English
Only engineers may view the results
The AI must be the cheapest option available
questions.explanation: Explainability means the reasoning behind AI outputs can be understood and communicated to stakeholders.

questions.q: If a donor requests raw AI chat logs containing identifiable beneficiary data, the responsible response is to:
options: Share only de-identified or aggregated information consistent with consent and privacy law
Share the logs immediately without review
Refuse to communicate with the donor at all
Delete all evidence of the evaluation
questions.explanation: Only de-identified or aggregated data consistent with consent and law should be shared, protecting beneficiaries' privacy.

questions.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023, a Data Principal generally has the right to:
options: Prevent all statistical research permanently
Take ownership of the Data Fiduciary's company
Access, correct, and request erasure of their personal data
Demand payment for every use of their data
questions.explanation: The DPDP Act grants Data Principals rights to access, correct, and seek erasure of their personal data.

questions.q: A responsible way to use AI for translating sensitive interview transcripts in South Asia is to:
options: Skip translation entirely to avoid all risk
Publish the untranslated transcripts publicly
De-identify first and use a vetted tool with clear data-handling terms
Use any free online translator with the real names included
questions.explanation: De-identifying transcripts and choosing a vetted tool with clear data terms reduces exposure of sensitive information.

questions.q: The concept of 'accountability gap' with AI in M&E refers to:
options: A shortage of AI subscriptions
A gap in the evaluation timeline
Difficulty assigning responsibility when an AI-influenced decision causes harm
The distance between two field offices
questions.explanation: The accountability gap is the difficulty in assigning clear responsibility when an AI-influenced decision leads to harm.

questions.q: Which is the BEST example of proactive transparency in an AI-assisted evaluation methodology section?
options: Stating which AI tools assisted coding, how outputs were verified, and known limitations
Omitting any mention of tools used
Claiming the AI is 100% accurate
Listing only the human authors
questions.explanation: Naming the AI tools, describing verification, and stating limitations is proactive, honest transparency.

questions.q: 'Data localization' concerns raised by the DPDP framework relate to:
options: Rules and safeguards on transferring personal data across borders to other countries
Translating data into local dialects
Storing data only on paper
Using local staff for data entry
questions.explanation: Data localization/cross-border transfer rules govern whether and how personal data may be sent outside the country.

questions.q: When an AI tool's terms state that inputs may be used to improve its models, an M&E practitioner should:
options: Avoid entering identifiable or sensitive data, or use an enterprise option that disables training
Ignore the terms because they are non-binding
Assume this is harmless and proceed with real data
Enter more data to speed up improvements
questions.explanation: If inputs feed model training, practitioners should withhold sensitive data or use a configuration that disables training on their data.

questions.q: A responsible-AI 'privacy by design' approach means:
options: Letting users opt into privacy later if they complain
Building privacy safeguards into systems and workflows from the outset
Designing the most visually attractive dashboards
Adding privacy protections only after a breach occurs
questions.explanation: Privacy by design embeds data-protection safeguards into systems and processes from the very beginning.

questions.q: Which scenario best illustrates a dual-use risk in evaluation data?
options: An evaluator uses two laptops
A vulnerability map built to target aid is leaked and used to target the same households for exploitation
A survey is conducted in two seasons
A report is printed in two colors
questions.explanation: A tool built to direct aid can be repurposed to harm the very people it mapped if it falls into the wrong hands.

questions.q: Why is obtaining consent for AI use sometimes described as an ongoing rather than one-time act?
options: Because respondents forget their answers
Because AI tools change their names frequently
Because consent forms expire every 24 hours by law
Because new AI uses or data sharing beyond the original purpose may require renewed consent
questions.explanation: If data will be used in new ways or shared beyond the original consented purpose, fresh consent is generally needed.

questions.q: The safest handling of a Personally Identifiable Information (PII) column before AI analysis is to:
options: Highlight it in red
Leave it in so the AI has full context
Replace it with pseudonymized codes held separately from the analysis dataset
Duplicate it for backup in the same file
questions.explanation: Pseudonymizing PII and keeping the key separate lets analysis proceed while protecting identities.

questions.q: Which is a valid limitation of relying on AI for sentiment analysis of beneficiary feedback in South Asia?
options: AI always understands every local language and dialect perfectly
AI cannot process text at all
AI sentiment analysis is legally prohibited everywhere
AI may misread cultural context, sarcasm, or low-resource languages, producing inaccurate results
questions.explanation: AI may misinterpret cultural nuance, sarcasm, and under-resourced South Asian languages, yielding unreliable sentiment scores.

questions.q: In responsible-AI governance, an 'AI impact assessment' before deployment aims to:
options: Calculate the tool's electricity bill only
Identify potential risks, harms, and mitigations before the tool is used on real data
Estimate the marketing reach of the tool
Rank staff by AI skill
questions.explanation: An AI impact assessment surfaces potential risks and harms and plans mitigations before real-world deployment.

questions.q: A common mistake that undermines de-identification is:
options: Removing all identifiers systematically
Leaving free-text fields that mention names, villages, or unique events unredacted
Using aggregated statistics
Storing the linkage key offline
questions.explanation: Unredacted free-text often contains names, places, and unique details that re-identify individuals despite structured-field cleaning.

questions.q: Which statement reflects responsible disclosure of AI limitations to decision-makers?
options: 'The AI findings are certain and require no verification'
'AI is infallible so we removed the human review'
'AI assisted the analysis; results were human-verified and may contain errors requiring judgment'
'We hid the AI use to keep the report simple'
questions.explanation: Responsibly stating that AI assisted, results were verified, and errors are possible helps decision-makers weigh the evidence appropriately.

questions.q: Under the do-no-harm principle, publishing disaggregated data on a small minority group is risky because:
options: It uses more ink
Minorities cannot read reports
Small cell sizes can enable identification and expose the group to stigma or reprisal
It is always illegal to disaggregate data
questions.explanation: Small subgroup counts can make individuals identifiable and expose vulnerable groups to stigma or reprisal.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a Data Processing Agreement (DPA) with an AI vendor?
options: To legally define how the vendor may handle, secure, and retain the personal data it processes
To grant the vendor ownership of all beneficiary data
To set the price of the subscription only
To waive the organization's privacy obligations
questions.explanation: A DPA contractually binds the vendor on how personal data is handled, secured, retained, and deleted.

questions.q: Which practice best embodies the responsible-AI principle of 'human agency and oversight'?
options: Removing all humans from the evaluation process
Letting AI auto-approve program funding decisions with no review
Ensuring humans can review, override, and take responsibility for AI-influenced decisions
Hiding AI recommendations from managers
questions.explanation: Human agency and oversight ensure people can review, override, and remain accountable for AI-influenced decisions.

questions.q: An evaluator notices an AI tool consistently rates women's feedback as less 'credible.' The responsible action is to:
options: Accept the ratings as objective
Apply the bias to speed up analysis
Delete all women's responses
Flag the potential gender bias, investigate, and avoid using the biased output in decisions
questions.explanation: Detecting and investigating biased outputs, and not relying on them, protects fairness and prevents discriminatory decisions.

questions.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023, if a data breach occurs, the Data Fiduciary is generally required to:
options: Ignore it unless someone complains
Notify the Data Protection Board and affected Data Principals
Pay each affected person a fixed bonus
Delete the company records
questions.explanation: The DPDP Act requires the Data Fiduciary to notify the Data Protection Board and affected Data Principals of a breach.

questions.q: Which is the most responsible way to store the mapping between pseudonymized codes and real identities?
options: Written on the report's cover page
In a separate, access-controlled and encrypted location apart from the analysis data
In a public shared folder for convenience
In the same spreadsheet uploaded to the AI tool
questions.explanation: Keeping the re-identification key encrypted and separate from analysis data limits who can re-link identities.

questions.q: The principle of 'proportionality' in using AI for surveillance-adjacent M&E means:
options: Proportioning the budget across staff
Using the largest possible AI model regardless of need
Monitoring everyone equally at all times
Ensuring data collection and monitoring intensity are justified by and proportionate to the purpose
questions.explanation: Proportionality requires that the intrusiveness of monitoring be justified by and not exceed what the legitimate purpose demands.

questions.q: Overall, the most defensible stance for M&E practitioners adopting AI is to:
options: Balance AI's benefits against privacy, equity, and do-no-harm risks with clear governance and human oversight
Use AI only to reduce staff costs
Adopt every new AI tool immediately without safeguards
Reject all AI regardless of context
questions.explanation: Responsible adoption weighs AI's benefits against privacy, equity, and harm risks, backed by governance and human oversight.

questions.q: Across the M&E cycle (design, data collection, cleaning, analysis, reporting, learning), where does AI tend to add the LEAST defensible value?
options: Making the final judgement on whether a program should be scaled or terminated
Speeding up qualitative coding of open-ended survey responses
Detecting outliers and inconsistencies during data cleaning
Drafting the first version of a results narrative
questions.explanation: High-stakes accountability decisions require human judgement, contextual knowledge, and legitimacy that AI cannot supply, so the final scale/terminate call should stay with people.

questions.q: What is the core idea of a 'human-in-the-loop' design for AI in evaluation?
options: Humans review, correct, and approve AI outputs before they are acted on
AI runs fully autonomously and humans only see the final report
Humans collect the data and AI does everything else unsupervised
AI is used only for tasks no human has ever done
questions.explanation: Human-in-the-loop keeps a person responsible for validating and approving AI outputs at key decision points, preserving accountability and catching errors.

questions.q: In the augmentation-versus-automation distinction, 'augmentation' means AI is used to:
options: Enhance and speed up a human's work while the human stays in control
Replace the evaluator entirely for a given task
Remove all manual steps from a workflow
Generate conclusions without any data
questions.explanation: Augmentation amplifies human capability and keeps the evaluator in charge, whereas automation hands the whole task to the machine.

questions.q: An M&E team must transcribe 200 hours of local-language focus-group recordings. Which is the strongest case for AI adoption?
options: A high-volume, repetitive, well-defined task where AI saves substantial time
A one-off task requiring deep contextual political judgement
A task where errors could directly harm respondents' safety
A task the team only does once a year for a handful of files
questions.explanation: AI pays off most on high-volume, repetitive, well-specified tasks like bulk transcription, where time savings are large and errors are correctable.

questions.q: When is a simpler NON-AI approach usually the better choice?
options: When a spreadsheet formula or pivot table already solves the problem reliably
When the dataset is far too large for any human to read
When qualitative text needs rapid thematic summarisation at scale
When you need to draft boilerplate report sections quickly
questions.explanation: If a deterministic, transparent tool like a spreadsheet already does the job, adding AI introduces cost and opacity without benefit.

questions.q: A key risk of AUTOMATING data cleaning end-to-end without human review is that:
options: Silent, systematic errors can propagate into all downstream analysis
Cleaning always becomes slower than doing it by hand
AI cannot detect any missing values
The raw data files are permanently deleted
questions.explanation: Fully automated cleaning can introduce consistent, invisible errors that then contaminate every subsequent analysis, so review checkpoints matter.

questions.q: Which factor should weigh MOST heavily when choosing an AI tool for evaluation work involving respondent data?
options: Data privacy, security, and where the data is processed and stored
Whether the tool has the most modern user interface
Whether competitors in the sector are using it
The number of social media followers the vendor has
questions.explanation: Handling respondent data responsibly makes privacy, security, and data residency the decisive selection criteria, especially under do-no-harm principles.

questions.q: 'Workflow integration' of an AI tool primarily refers to:
options: How well the tool fits existing processes, formats, and systems the team already uses
How many AI models the tool can access at once
Whether the tool has a mobile app
The tool's marketing partnerships
questions.explanation: Integration is about the tool slotting into current data formats, systems, and staff routines rather than forcing a disruptive parallel process.

questions.q: A cost-benefit assessment of adopting an AI tool should count which as a REAL cost beyond the subscription fee?
options: Staff time for training, prompt design, and output verification
The electricity used by respondents' phones
The cost of printing the final report
The vendor's own R&D budget
questions.explanation: Total cost of ownership includes the substantial human time for onboarding, prompting, and checking outputs, not just the licence price.

questions.q: In change management for AI adoption, the most common reason a rollout fails is:
options: Staff resistance and lack of trust or skills, not the technology itself
The AI model being too accurate
Having too much documentation
Choosing open-source over proprietary tools
questions.explanation: Adoption failures are usually organisational and human (fear, low trust, and missing skills) rather than technical shortcomings.

questions.q: Which task in the evaluation cycle is BEST suited to AI augmentation rather than full automation?
options: Interpreting why a result occurred and what it means for stakeholders
Converting audio recordings into rough text drafts
Flagging duplicate rows in a dataset
Generating a first-draft literature summary
questions.explanation: Interpretation and sense-making need human context and accountability, so AI should assist the evaluator rather than replace them.

questions.q: An indicator-heavy quarterly report is produced identically every quarter. The best AI role here is to:
options: Automate the templated narrative while staff verify the figures
Decide which indicators the program should track
Replace the M&E officer's judgement on data quality
Choose the program's strategic priorities
questions.explanation: Routine, templated reporting is a good automation candidate, but humans still verify the underlying numbers and keep strategic judgement.

questions.q: Why is 'accuracy on your own data' more important than a tool's advertised benchmark scores?
options: Benchmarks may not reflect your languages, contexts, or data types
Benchmarks are always falsified by vendors
Your data can never be tested
Benchmark scores change every day
questions.explanation: General benchmarks rarely capture South Asian languages, local contexts, or your specific data, so pilot testing on real data is essential.

questions.q: A responsible way to introduce AI into an M&E team is to:
options: Pilot on a low-risk task, measure results, then expand gradually
Replace all analysts immediately to maximise savings
Mandate AI for every task with no exceptions
Adopt it silently without telling staff
questions.explanation: Phased piloting on low-risk tasks builds trust, surfaces problems early, and lets the team learn before scaling up.

questions.q: In the 'learning' phase of M&E, AI is most appropriately used to:
options: Surface patterns and questions for humans to reflect on and validate
Automatically decide the organisation's next strategy
Replace participatory reflection sessions entirely
Set staff performance ratings
questions.explanation: AI can help spot patterns and prompt reflection, but the collaborative sense-making and strategic decisions stay with people.

questions.q: Which is a defensible reason to REJECT an otherwise capable AI tool?
options: Its terms allow the vendor to train on your confidential respondent data
It is faster than the current manual method
It integrates with your existing spreadsheet software
It offers a free tier for small teams
questions.explanation: If the vendor can train models on sensitive respondent data, that violates confidentiality commitments regardless of the tool's speed.

questions.q: 'Automation bias' in an AI-assisted evaluation workflow refers to the tendency to:
options: Over-trust AI outputs and skip the human verification step
Refuse to use any automated tools
Prefer manual data entry for its own sake
Automate only the hardest tasks
questions.explanation: Automation bias is the human habit of accepting machine outputs uncritically, which is exactly why verification checkpoints are built in.

questions.q: When mapping AI to the DESIGN phase of an evaluation, a sensible use is:
options: Brainstorming indicator options and draft survey questions for expert review
Finalising the sampling frame without statistical review
Deciding the evaluation's ethical boundaries autonomously
Approving the budget
questions.explanation: AI can generate draft indicators and questions to accelerate design, but methodological and ethical decisions require expert human judgement.

questions.q: A small NGO has 3 surveys a year and no data staff. The cost-benefit of a paid enterprise AI analytics platform is likely:
options: Unfavourable: low volume means the fixed cost outweighs the benefit
Always favourable because AI is cheap
Irrelevant because AI is mandatory
Favourable only if the surveys are in English
questions.explanation: AI investments pay off through volume; for a handful of surveys, the setup and licence costs typically exceed the time saved.

questions.q: Which practice best preserves accountability when AI drafts an evaluation report?
options: A named human reviews, edits, and signs off on the final content
The AI's output is published verbatim to save time
The vendor guarantees the content is correct
The draft is emailed directly to funders unread
questions.explanation: A human editor who reviews, corrects, and takes responsibility for the final report keeps accountability with the organisation.

questions.q: Why can AI hallucination be especially dangerous in the ANALYSIS phase?
options: It can invent plausible-sounding findings or figures that are false
It slows the analysis to an unusable speed
It deletes the raw dataset automatically
It only affects spelling, never numbers
questions.explanation: Hallucinated statistics or findings look credible but are fabricated, so unverified AI analysis can mislead decisions.

questions.q: The most useful first question before adopting any AI tool for a task is:
options: What specific problem are we solving, and does AI actually solve it better?
Which tool is the newest on the market?
What do our peer organisations subscribe to?
How advanced is the underlying model?
questions.explanation: Starting from the concrete problem prevents technology-led adoption where a tool is bought before a real need is defined.

questions.q: In a human-in-the-loop transcription workflow for local languages, the human's key job is to:
options: Correct mistranscriptions, especially names, numbers, and dialect terms
Re-record every interview from scratch
Translate the audio before the AI sees it
Delete recordings the AI finds difficult
questions.explanation: AI transcription of low-resource languages struggles with names, figures, and dialect, so human correction targets exactly those error-prone elements.

questions.q: Which is a sign that a workflow has been over-automated?
options: Errors are discovered late because no one reviews intermediate steps
Staff spend too long verifying every output
The team refuses to use the tool
The tool produces outputs slowly
questions.explanation: When review checkpoints are stripped out to maximise speed, mistakes surface only downstream: a hallmark of over-automation.

questions.q: For capacity building around AI in M&E, the highest-leverage skill to develop is:
options: Critical verification: knowing how to check and challenge AI outputs
Memorising every AI model's release date
Typing prompts as fast as possible
Coding a large language model from scratch
questions.explanation: Practitioners add the most value by critically appraising AI outputs, so verification literacy is the priority skill to build.

questions.q: A funder asks whether AI was used in an evaluation. The best practice is to:
options: Disclose transparently how and where AI was used and how outputs were checked
Deny any AI use to appear more rigorous
Refuse to answer as it is proprietary
Only mention it if directly proven
questions.explanation: Transparent disclosure of AI use and the verification steps taken maintains trust and lets stakeholders judge reliability.

questions.q: Which of these is genuinely a poor fit for AI in the data-collection phase?
options: Judging in real time whether a vulnerable respondent should continue an interview
Auto-suggesting skip-logic in a digital survey form
Flagging implausible entries as they are typed
Translating a questionnaire draft for review
questions.explanation: Ethical, in-the-moment decisions about a vulnerable respondent's welfare require human sensitivity that AI cannot responsibly provide.

questions.q: 'Total cost of ownership' for an AI tool is best described as:
options: Licence plus training, integration, verification, and maintenance over time
Only the monthly subscription price
The vendor's list price minus any discount
The one-time cost of the first prompt
questions.explanation: TCO captures all recurring human and system costs, not just the sticker price, giving a realistic view of affordability.

questions.q: When AI is used to code qualitative data, the recommended safeguard is:
options: Human coders validate a sample and reconcile disagreements with the AI
Accept all AI codes without review to stay consistent
Never let humans see the AI's coding scheme
Discard any quotes the AI cannot code
questions.explanation: Validating a sample and reconciling human-AI disagreements keeps the coding trustworthy while still gaining efficiency.

questions.q: Which statement about 'AI for everything' as a strategy is correct?
options: It wastes resources on tasks where simpler tools work better
It always maximises efficiency
It is required by most donors
It removes the need for any staff skills
questions.explanation: Blanket AI adoption ignores that many tasks are solved more cheaply and transparently by conventional tools.

questions.q: A team notices AI summaries consistently omit the perspectives of a minority-language subgroup. This signals:
options: A representation gap that needs human oversight and correction
That the subgroup's data should be dropped
That the AI is working as intended
That summaries should be fully automated
questions.explanation: Systematic omission of a subgroup is a bias/representation failure that demands human review to avoid excluding those voices.

questions.q: In deciding augmentation vs automation for a task, a key test is:
options: How costly and reversible are the errors if the AI is wrong?
How impressive the AI demo looked
Whether the vendor recommends automation
How many features the tool has
questions.explanation: Tasks with costly or irreversible errors call for augmentation with human checks; low-stakes, reversible tasks can be more fully automated.

questions.q: Which is the best example of AI augmenting the REPORTING phase appropriately?
options: Suggesting clearer phrasing and structure that the author then edits
Publishing the AI's draft without any human edit
Choosing which findings to hide from funders
Fabricating quotes to strengthen the narrative
questions.explanation: AI can improve clarity and structure as a drafting aid, with the human author retaining editorial control and integrity.

questions.q: A realistic barrier to AI adoption specific to South Asian M&E contexts is:
options: Limited support for local languages and unreliable connectivity
Too many staff already expert in AI
An oversupply of high-quality local-language models
Excessive donor funding for AI tools
questions.explanation: Low-resource language support and connectivity constraints are practical, region-specific limits that shape which AI tools are viable.

questions.q: Why is documenting your AI workflow (prompts, tools, checks) important?
options: It makes the process reproducible, auditable, and correctable
It guarantees the AI will never make errors
It replaces the need for data validation
It lets you avoid disclosing AI use
questions.explanation: Documentation supports reproducibility and audit, letting others understand, verify, and improve how AI was used.

questions.q: An evaluator wants to detect anomalies in a large monitoring dataset. The soundest approach is:
options: Use AI to flag candidates, then have an analyst investigate each flag
Let AI delete anomalous rows automatically
Ignore anomalies since AI would find them later
Assume all AI-flagged rows are true errors
questions.explanation: AI is good at surfacing candidate anomalies, but a human must investigate before any row is corrected or removed.

questions.q: Which best captures 'right tool for the task' thinking?
options: Matching the tool's strengths and risks to the task's needs and stakes
Always picking the most powerful general-purpose model
Standardising on one tool for every task
Choosing whatever is cheapest regardless of fit
questions.explanation: Fit-for-purpose selection weighs each task's requirements and risk level against a tool's specific strengths and limitations.

questions.q: A danger of letting AI both generate AND evaluate its own analysis is:
options: There is no independent check, so errors go undetected
It doubles the processing cost only
It always produces slower results
It prevents any output from being generated
questions.explanation: Self-evaluation lacks independence; an external human or separate check is needed to catch the AI's own mistakes.

questions.q: When building staff buy-in for AI, an effective early step is to:
options: Show a concrete, relevant win that saves the team real time
Threaten job cuts to force adoption
Ban all existing manual methods immediately
Keep the tool restricted to senior managers
questions.explanation: Demonstrating a tangible, relevant time-saving win builds trust and motivation far better than coercion or exclusivity.

questions.q: Which is TRUE about AI and small qualitative datasets (e.g., 12 interviews)?
options: A skilled human can often analyse them well without AI
AI is always faster and better for tiny datasets
Human analysis is impossible below 50 interviews
AI removes the need to read the transcripts
questions.explanation: For small qualitative sets, close human reading is feasible and often richer, so AI may add little beyond convenience.

questions.q: The safest way to handle sensitive respondent identifiers with a cloud AI tool is to:
options: De-identify or anonymise data before it is sent to the tool
Send raw data and trust the vendor's privacy policy
Include names to improve the AI's accuracy
Skip consent since AI processing is automatic
questions.explanation: Removing or masking identifiers before uploading limits exposure and upholds confidentiality even if the vendor is trusted.

questions.q: 'Change management' in AI adoption is mainly about:
options: Guiding people and processes through the transition to new ways of working
Changing the AI model every few weeks
Managing the electricity supply for servers
Editing the source code of the AI
questions.explanation: Change management addresses the human and organisational shift (roles, skills, trust, and processes) that new tools require.

questions.q: Which scenario most justifies FULL automation with light monitoring?
options: Nightly reformatting of clean data into a fixed dashboard layout
Deciding whether a pilot program met its objectives
Interpreting contradictory stakeholder feedback
Judging the credibility of a whistle-blower account
questions.explanation: A repetitive, low-stakes, well-defined formatting task is a strong automation candidate needing only occasional monitoring.

questions.q: A red flag that a team is adopting AI for the wrong reasons is:
options: Buying a tool because it is trendy rather than to solve a defined problem
Piloting a tool on a small, low-risk task first
Comparing several tools against real data
Budgeting for staff training
questions.explanation: Hype-driven adoption without a defined problem is a classic pitfall, unlike the sound practices of piloting and problem-first selection.

questions.q: Why should evaluators be cautious using AI to write the METHODOLOGY section?
options: AI may misstate what was actually done, so it must match real procedures
Methodology sections cannot contain any AI text
AI always describes methods more rigorously than humans
Funders forbid any AI-written methods
questions.explanation: The methodology must faithfully describe the actual process; AI drafts can introduce inaccuracies that misrepresent what was really done.

questions.q: Which measure best tells you whether an AI tool is worth keeping after a pilot?
options: Net time saved and quality achieved versus the manual baseline
The number of AI features it advertises
How many other NGOs have heard of it
The size of the model's training data
questions.explanation: Evaluating the pilot against a manual baseline on time and quality gives an evidence-based keep-or-drop decision.

questions.q: In a mixed team, an equitable capacity approach to AI is to:
options: Train all relevant staff, not just tech-savvy individuals
Concentrate AI skills in one gatekeeper
Assume junior staff cannot learn the tools
Only train staff who already code
questions.explanation: Broad-based training spreads capability and avoids a single point of dependency, making AI use more resilient and equitable.

questions.q: What is the main limitation of using AI to generate 'insights' directly from data?
options: It can produce confident but context-blind or spurious conclusions
It never finds any patterns
It only works on numeric data
It always requires a supercomputer
questions.explanation: AI lacks program context and can mistake noise for signal, so its 'insights' need human interpretation and validation.

questions.q: When integrating AI into an established M&E system, the least disruptive strategy is to:
options: Add AI at specific steps while keeping proven processes intact
Rebuild the entire system around the AI at once
Discard all existing tools immediately
Run AI only in a completely separate silo forever
questions.explanation: Targeted insertion at specific steps preserves what works and reduces risk, compared with a wholesale rip-and-replace.

questions.q: The overarching principle for AI across the M&E cycle is best summarised as:
options: AI assists and accelerates; humans stay accountable for judgement and ethics
AI should replace human evaluators wherever possible
AI removes the need for M&E frameworks
AI eliminates all bias from evaluation
questions.explanation: The guiding principle is augmentation with human accountability: AI speeds the work while people own judgement, ethics, and final decisions.

questions.q: In the context of large language models, what does 'hallucination' refer to?
options: The model refusing to answer a question
The model generating plausible-sounding but factually false or fabricated information
The model running slowly under heavy load
The model producing images instead of text
questions.explanation: AI hallucination is when a model confidently generates content that is fabricated or inaccurate while appearing credible.

questions.q: An M&E officer asks an AI chatbot for a citation to support a claim in an evaluation report, and it produces a realistic-looking journal reference that does not actually exist. This is an example of:
options: Model drift
Automation bias
Reproducibility failure
Confabulation of a fake citation
questions.explanation: Fabricating non-existent references is a classic confabulation, so every AI-supplied citation must be independently verified.

questions.q: 'Automation bias' in the use of AI tools most accurately describes the tendency to:
options: Automate as many M&E tasks as possible
Prefer manual data entry over software
Bias a dataset during automated cleaning
Over-trust and uncritically accept outputs from an automated system
questions.explanation: Automation bias is the human tendency to defer to machine-generated recommendations even when they are wrong.

questions.q: Why are many deep-learning models described as 'black boxes'?
options: They can only be run on black-coloured servers
They store data in an encrypted black file
Their internal reasoning for a given output is not readily interpretable by humans
They only work with black-and-white images
questions.explanation: Black-box models produce outputs without a transparent, human-readable explanation of how they reached them.

questions.q: Which situation is the STRONGEST reason NOT to rely on a generative AI tool for an M&E task?
options: Making a final beneficiary-eligibility decision that affects people's welfare with no human review
Drafting a first outline of a report section
Suggesting synonyms for a survey question
Brainstorming possible indicators for later expert vetting
questions.explanation: High-stakes decisions affecting people's rights or welfare should not be delegated to an unaccountable AI without human oversight.

questions.q: 'Triangulation' as a verification strategy for AI outputs means:
options: Running the same prompt three times
Using three different AI models simultaneously
Drawing a triangle diagram of the results
Cross-checking a finding against multiple independent sources or methods
questions.explanation: Triangulation confirms a finding by corroborating it across independent data sources, methods, or evaluators.

questions.q: What is the best first step when an AI summarises a set of qualitative interview transcripts for an evaluation?
options: Spot-check the summary against the original transcripts for accuracy
Publish the summary directly in the report
Delete the raw transcripts to save space
Assume it is accurate because the AI processed all the data
questions.explanation: AI summaries can omit or distort content, so validating against source transcripts is essential before use.

questions.q: 'Model drift' refers to:
options: A model physically moving between servers
The model slowly increasing in file size
Random variation in a model's response speed
Degradation of a model's performance over time as real-world data diverges from its training data
questions.explanation: Model drift occurs when the statistical patterns a model learned no longer match current conditions, reducing accuracy.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST supports reproducibility when AI is used in an evaluation?
options: Keeping the prompts and methods secret
Using a different model each time to avoid bias
Documenting the model version, prompts, and parameters used
Only reporting the final numbers
questions.explanation: Recording the exact model, prompts, and settings lets others reproduce and audit the AI-assisted analysis.

questions.q: 'Red-teaming' an AI output in an evaluation context means:
options: Colour-coding results in red for emphasis
Assigning a red-alert priority to the task
Deliberately probing and challenging the output to expose errors, biases, or weaknesses
Having a marketing team review it
questions.explanation: Red-teaming adversarially stress-tests AI outputs to find flaws before they cause harm in decision-making.

questions.q: An evaluator notices an AI-generated statistic that seems too precise and cannot be traced to any dataset. The most responsible action is to:
options: Exclude it until it can be verified against a primary source
Include it with a footnote saying 'AI-generated'
Round it to make it look more credible
Ask the AI to confirm it is correct
questions.explanation: Unverifiable AI statistics should be excluded, since asking the model to self-confirm does not establish truth.

questions.q: Why is asking an AI model 'Are you sure this is correct?' an UNRELIABLE way to verify a factual claim?
options: The model's confidence is not a reliable indicator of factual accuracy
The model always says yes
It costs extra money
The model cannot understand the question
questions.explanation: LLMs can express high confidence in false statements, so self-assessment is not a substitute for external verification.

questions.q: Over-reliance on AI-generated indicators in an M&E framework primarily risks:
options: Faster reporting cycles
Lower software licensing costs
Embedding plausible but contextually inappropriate or unmeasurable indicators
Improved stakeholder engagement
questions.explanation: AI may propose generic indicators that sound reasonable but do not fit the local context or measurement capacity.

questions.q: Which practice most directly reduces automation bias in a team using AI for coding qualitative data?
options: Having human coders independently verify a sample and reconcile disagreements
Letting the AI code all data unsupervised
Trusting the AI because it is consistent
Increasing the dataset size
questions.explanation: Independent human verification and reconciliation counteracts the tendency to accept AI codes without scrutiny.

questions.q: A key limitation of using AI to analyse data in low-resource South Asian languages is that:
options: It always translates perfectly
Models are often under-trained on these languages, increasing error and bias
It cannot process any non-English text
It is slower but equally accurate
questions.explanation: Many models have limited high-quality training data for low-resource languages, raising the risk of errors and bias.

questions.q: For accountability, documentation of AI use in an evaluation should include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Which tasks used AI and which did not
The personal opinions of the AI about the project
The prompts and model version used
How outputs were verified
questions.explanation: AI documentation covers tasks, tools, and verification methods; a model has no genuine opinions to record.

questions.q: Which scenario is MOST appropriate for AI assistance in M&E?
options: Generating a draft codebook that human analysts then refine
Signing off on the final impact claim
Replacing the entire evaluation team
Deciding which communities receive aid
questions.explanation: AI is well suited to producing drafts that humans review and improve, not to making final accountable decisions.

questions.q: 'Explainability' (or interpretability) of an AI model matters in M&E mainly because:
options: It makes reports longer
Stakeholders need to understand and challenge how conclusions were reached
It speeds up model training
It reduces electricity use
questions.explanation: Explainable outputs allow stakeholders to scrutinise, trust, and contest AI-informed evaluation conclusions.

questions.q: A predictive model built in 2021 to flag at-risk students now performs poorly because enrolment patterns changed after the pandemic. This is an example of:
options: Hallucination
Automation bias
Model drift
Red-teaming
questions.explanation: Changing real-world conditions since training caused the model's accuracy to degrade, the definition of model drift.

questions.q: The safest way to treat any single AI output used in an evaluation is as:
options: A draft or hypothesis requiring human verification
Final, authoritative evidence
Irrelevant and to be ignored
A legally binding conclusion
questions.explanation: AI outputs are best treated as provisional inputs that must be checked before informing decisions.

questions.q: Which is a warning sign that an AI-generated data analysis may be unreliable?
options: It cites verifiable primary sources
The numbers cannot be reproduced from the underlying dataset
It matches the manual calculation
It flags its own uncertainty
questions.explanation: If AI results cannot be reproduced from the raw data, they may be fabricated or miscomputed and should not be trusted.

questions.q: 'Confabulation' differs subtly from a simple error because it involves:
options: The model deliberately lying with intent
A hardware malfunction
A user typing the wrong prompt
The model generating fluent, self-consistent but invented details
questions.explanation: Confabulation is the fluent generation of invented content without intent, filling gaps with plausible fabrication.

questions.q: When an AI tool is used to clean survey data, reproducibility is best protected by:
options: Doing the cleaning interactively without saving steps
Trusting the AI to remember what it did
Logging the exact cleaning rules and version so the process can be re-run
Deleting the original raw data
questions.explanation: A documented, versioned cleaning script allows the same transformations to be reproduced and audited later.

questions.q: A donor asks how you ensured an AI-assisted analysis was trustworthy. The strongest answer references:
options: A verification protocol with human review and triangulation
The AI's popularity
The speed of the tool
The brand of the AI company
questions.explanation: Trustworthiness rests on documented verification, human oversight, and triangulation, not on the tool's reputation.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a recognised limitation of current generative AI for M&E?
options: It can fabricate facts and citations
It can guarantee 100% accurate causal inference
It can reflect biases in its training data
Its performance can drift over time
questions.explanation: AI cannot guarantee accurate causal inference; the other three are well-documented limitations.

questions.q: Automation bias is especially dangerous when:
options: The user is a domain expert who double-checks everything
The task is trivial and low-risk
Multiple independent reviewers disagree with the AI
The output is highly stakes-relevant and users defer to it without independent checks
questions.explanation: Uncritical deference to AI on high-stakes decisions is where automation bias causes the most harm.

questions.q: A robust way to detect AI hallucination in a literature review is to:
options: Trust the fluency of the writing
Count the number of citations
Ask the AI to rate its own accuracy
Independently locate and read each cited source
questions.explanation: Verifying that each cited source genuinely exists and says what is claimed is the reliable defence against hallucinated references.

questions.q: Why should evaluators be cautious about using AI to infer causation from observational program data?
options: Correlation detected by AI does not establish causation without proper design
AI is too slow for causal analysis
AI cannot process numbers
Causal inference is illegal
questions.explanation: AI may surface correlations, but valid causal claims require appropriate evaluation designs and assumptions.

questions.q: The main purpose of keeping a 'prompt log' when using AI in evaluations is to:
options: Impress stakeholders
Reduce the cost of the AI subscription
Enable transparency and reproducibility of AI-assisted work
Train a new model
questions.explanation: A prompt log documents exactly how outputs were produced so the work can be reviewed and reproduced.

questions.q: Which is the clearest example of appropriate human-in-the-loop verification?
options: Auto-publishing AI findings to the public dashboard
Letting the AI approve its own outputs
Removing all human reviewers to save time
An analyst reviewing and correcting AI-coded responses before analysis
questions.explanation: Human-in-the-loop means a person reviews and can override AI outputs before they are used.

questions.q: An AI model trained mostly on urban data is used to evaluate a rural livelihoods program. The primary risk is:
options: The model will run faster
Systematic bias and poor fit to the rural context
Reduced electricity consumption
Better accuracy in villages
questions.explanation: Training data that does not represent the target population produces biased, context-inappropriate outputs.

questions.q: Reproducibility of AI-assisted results is threatened MOST when:
options: An updated model silently changes outputs for the same prompt
Model versions and settings are recorded
The same fixed prompt and seed are reused
The analysis code is shared openly
questions.explanation: Silent model updates can change outputs for identical prompts, breaking reproducibility unless versions are pinned and documented.

questions.q: In red-teaming an AI-generated evaluation finding, a useful question is:
options: Does this finding sound impressive?
How quickly was it produced?
What evidence would contradict this, and did the AI consider it?
Which font should we use?
questions.explanation: Red-teaming actively searches for disconfirming evidence and overlooked alternatives to test a finding's robustness.

questions.q: Which statement about AI confidence and accuracy is TRUE?
options: High confidence always means high accuracy
Low confidence always means the answer is wrong
Confidence scores are legally verified
A model can state falsehoods with high apparent confidence
questions.explanation: LLMs can present incorrect information assertively, so apparent confidence is not evidence of correctness.

questions.q: The precautionary principle applied to AI in M&E suggests that, when potential harm is high and verification is difficult, you should:
options: Deploy the AI widely to learn fast
Ignore the risk
Limit or avoid AI use until safeguards and verification are in place
Let the AI decide the safeguards
questions.explanation: Where harms are serious and hard to verify, restraint and safeguards are the responsible default.

questions.q: Which is the best way to guard against over-reliance on a single AI model?
options: Use only that one model for consistency
Increase the temperature setting
Cross-validate key outputs with other methods, models, or human experts
Run the model more times
questions.explanation: Cross-validation against independent methods and experts reduces dependence on any single fallible model.

questions.q: An evaluation report states 'AI was used to assist thematic coding, with 20% of codes manually verified.' This disclosure primarily supports:
options: Marketing the report
Hiding the use of AI
Increasing the word count
Transparency about AI's role and its verification
questions.explanation: Disclosing how and to what extent AI was used and verified upholds methodological transparency.

questions.q: Which of these tasks is LEAST suitable for unsupervised AI in a rigorous evaluation?
options: Generating a first draft of interview themes for review
Determining the final attribution of impact to the program
Formatting a bibliography
Suggesting alternative phrasings for a survey item
questions.explanation: Final impact attribution is a high-stakes analytical judgement that should not be left to unsupervised AI.

questions.q: A team finds that an AI consistently rates a particular ethnic group's feedback more negatively. This is most likely due to:
options: Model drift
A hallucination
Bias inherited from training data
Automation bias in the AI
questions.explanation: Systematic differential treatment of a group typically reflects biases embedded in the model's training data.

questions.q: The safest interpretation of an AI tool that lacks explainability for a critical decision is that it:
options: Should be trusted because it is advanced
Requires additional human judgement and validation before acting
Can replace the evaluation team
Is automatically compliant with ethics standards
questions.explanation: Opaque tools used for critical decisions demand extra human validation because their reasoning cannot be inspected.

questions.q: Which is a strong sign that AI verification processes are working in an M&E team?
options: Errors in AI output are routinely caught and corrected before publication
AI outputs are never questioned
The team has stopped reading source data
All decisions are made by the AI
questions.explanation: A functioning verification process regularly detects and fixes AI errors before they reach final products.

questions.q: Why is documenting 'what AI was NOT used for' also valuable in an evaluation?
options: It wastes space
It hides the AI use
It is required by the AI vendor
It clarifies the boundaries of AI involvement and human accountability
questions.explanation: Stating where AI was not used delineates human responsibility and the scope of AI's influence on findings.

questions.q: A practitioner wants to use AI to generate qualitative quotes to 'illustrate' findings. This is problematic because:
options: It is too slow
Fabricated quotes misrepresent real participants and violate research integrity
AI cannot write quotes
It uses too much data
questions.explanation: Inventing participant quotes fabricates evidence and breaches ethical and research-integrity standards.

questions.q: Which approach best addresses model drift for an AI tool used repeatedly over a multi-year program?
options: Assume the model stays accurate forever
Never update the model
Delete performance logs
Periodically re-validate the model against fresh ground-truth data
questions.explanation: Regular re-validation against current ground-truth data detects and corrects drift over time.

questions.q: The phrase 'garbage in, garbage out' applied to AI in M&E emphasises that:
options: AI improves any data automatically
Data must be physically discarded
Poor-quality input data yields unreliable AI outputs
AI only works with clean data
questions.explanation: AI outputs are only as trustworthy as the data fed in; flawed inputs produce flawed conclusions.

questions.q: When triangulating an AI-derived conclusion, which combination is STRONGEST?
options: Re-running the same AI prompt several times
Asking the AI to grade itself
Comparing the AI finding with administrative data and field observations
Reading only the AI's summary
questions.explanation: Corroborating an AI finding with genuinely independent sources like admin data and field observation is true triangulation.

questions.q: A responsible AI-use policy for an M&E unit should require, at minimum:
options: Human review of AI outputs, disclosure of AI use, and verification procedures
Unlimited unsupervised AI decision-making
Banning all documentation
Trusting outputs without checks to save time
questions.explanation: Sound policy mandates human oversight, transparency, and verification as baseline safeguards.

questions.q: Which is the MOST accurate statement about AI and sensitive personal data in evaluations?
options: Any AI tool can safely process personal data
Privacy rules do not apply to AI
Anonymisation is unnecessary with AI
Sharing identifiable data with external AI services can create serious privacy and consent risks
questions.explanation: Feeding identifiable data into external AI services can breach privacy, consent, and data-protection obligations.

questions.q: An analyst gets two contradictory answers from the same AI on the same question asked twice. The best conclusion is that:
options: The second answer is always right
AI outputs can be non-deterministic and must be independently verified
The AI is broken and unusable
The first answer is always right
questions.explanation: Variability across identical prompts shows outputs are not deterministic ground truth and require external verification.

questions.q: Overall, the most defensible stance for an M&E practitioner toward AI tools is to treat them as:
options: Infallible oracles
Powerful but fallible assistants whose outputs require verification and human judgement
Useless and to be avoided entirely
Legal decision-makers
questions.explanation: AI is best used as a fallible aid subject to human verification and judgement, neither blindly trusted nor wholly rejected.
